title: Ask HN: Which TV do you recommend for privacy?
body_text: Ask HN: Which TV do you recommend for privacy? | Hacker News Hacker News new | past | comments | ask | show | jobs | submit login Ask HN: Which TV do you recommend for privacy? 690 points by LecroJS 1 day ago | hide | past | favorite | 835 comments I haven’t owned a TV in years and would like one that respects my privacy. Are there any TV’s which do this well? I am looking for something in the 60”to 80”range and would like a 4k display with at least 60hz display. I don’t mind paying a premium. I have heard good things about Apple TV as a better alternative to most smart TV native apps. Would some TV’s pair better with this than others for privacy? I don’t want the TV doing anything other than being the display for Apple TV. I am curious what success others have had.   help MegaDeKay 1 day ago | next [–] - Buy an LG OLED TV. They're as gorgeous as they are notorious. I just got a 77" LG C6 and it is crazy good. - Root it [0]. - Install Glasshouse [1] and disable all telemetry. YOU now own the glass. Now you can chromecast to the TV, use Adfree YouTube, access IP TV, etc etc etc. No point crippling your TV by pulling the wireless module and voiding your warranty. - Install a bunch of cool apps to your TV [2] (there are many more out there besides those listed here) - Restore to Factory Defaults if you ever want / need to unroot and get back to stock e.g. a warranty claim The only issue is that LG recently closed the vulnerability that made rooting possible so you don't want any firmware released after 2026-10-10 like 43.21.84. Hopefully a new exploit is found that makes rooting possible once again. BTW, you might have heard of Dev Mode on these TVs but they don't allow anywhere near the functionality that rooting provides. [0] https://tv.slada.sk/guides/rooting-guide [1] https://github.com/rorygallagher2024/glasshouse [2] https://www.webosbrew.org/ reply andrewla 13 hours ago | parent | next [–] This seems excessive. Easier to disconnect it from the internet completely, and have it boot to HDMI1, hook up an external HDMI-CEC switch, and never think about it again. With "Hotel Mode" you can make this effectively permanent and never see LG's UI again unless you want it. Then just connect whatever HDMI-based box you want (Roku, Apple TV, Plex, Android, whatever) and use that for the content. reply vargr616 13 hours ago | root | parent | next [–] i personally wouldn't trust these not to spy on you even disconnected. They can still scan for networks and bluetooth devices around you reply jayknight 11 hours ago | root | parent | next [–] It won't be long until they have their own cellular modem so they don't need your network at all of the spying parts. reply c0n5pir4cy 10 hours ago | root | parent | next [–] I used to work for an IoT connectivity provider (think SIM cards, eUICC etc); I know that some of the manufacturers of various devices have been investigating adding cellular and soldered eUICC (ostensibly for diagnostics, warranty etc). So it's not even that it won't be long; I'm sure they already have designs and are just waiting for eUICC support to catch up. reply taurath 8 hours ago | root | parent | next [–] Vehicles already have them, you don't need a lot of bandwidth just enough data to identify the members household which can be done with a wifi access point map and bluetooth MACs. reply KerrAvon 9 hours ago | root | parent | prev | next [–] Then they'll quickly discover how bad cell coverage is in vast swathes of the USA and they'll have to be a lot more tolerant of bad customer sat scores and high return rates than they typically want to be. reply inemesitaffia 10 hours ago | root | parent | prev | next [–] The Qualcomm license probably makes it too expensive reply anjel 9 hours ago | root | parent | prev | next [–] Unless they include armored cellular antennas, it's just another thing to get defeated reply s3p 11 hours ago | root | parent | prev | next [–] where would they send that info without internet? reply 6thbit 10 hours ago | root | parent | next [–] - neighbor's open wifi - open hotspot - public city wifi close by reply qlte 9 hours ago | root | parent | next [–] I haven't seen an open WiFi network near any apartment I've lived in for more than a decade. There has never been a shred of evidence for any TV model actually doing this despite how often it's speculated about in comment sections. It's kinda weird how the most sensible, straightforward mitigation for the TV spying people claim to be concerned always gets this evidence-free FUD thrown out to claim it's pointless. reply 6thbit 9 hours ago | root | parent | next [–] Some people here say they have seen their TVs connecting https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=25275753 I have seen open wifi reachable from places i've lived on. Spotty and intermittent connection but there. Apartment buildings with businesses on the 1st floor are also common now, those businesses may have open wifi, etc. reply TranquilMarmot 8 hours ago | root | parent | prev | next [–] That's it, turning my apartment into a faraday cage reply PaulDavisThe1st 9 hours ago | root | parent | prev | next [–] yay for rural new mexico ... reply 6thbit 9 hours ago | root | parent | next [–] well air gapped reply snickerbockers 13 hours ago | root | parent | prev | next [–] Don't you then have to secure whatever you just plugged into the tv so it doesn't do the exact same thing??? reply andrewla 12 hours ago | root | parent | next [–] Yes, but you can choose your adventure here. Better than having to replace the entire TV if you find one that doesn't do what you want. Not to mention that technology moves forward and you can replace these if new models come out that have better features or are more aligned with your privacy preferences. reply revengerwizard 10 hours ago | root | parent | prev | next [–] You kind of leave all the compute that the TV has built-in basically unused reply HoldOnAMinute 9 hours ago | root | parent | next [–] Nobody wants compute in their TV. Its job is to do an exact reproduction of the HDMI digital incoming signal with no interpretation. reply revengerwizard 8 hours ago | root | parent | next [–] Don't get me wrong, I'm all for it; but, if you're buying a "smart" TV, you might as well use the processor present in it. Rooting it and what not. I guess I should have specified this. reply Banditoz 10 hours ago | root | parent | prev | next [–] Isn't that the point? You have no control over said compute. reply Henchman21 9 hours ago | root | parent | prev | next [–] Its a display reply eecc 13 hours ago | root | parent | prev | next [–] Nope. The TV stores all the data it harvests and scans WiFi in search of an open network. Whenever it finds one (and LG could make commercial agreements with Telco operating open WiFi’s to use them) it will connect and exfiltrate whatever it found. It’s malicious. reply shawabawa3 12 hours ago | root | parent | next [–] This has been mentioned in so many comments and there isn't a shred of evidence about it It seems to be misconstruing the fact that TVs will scan nearby networks for fingerprinting, but they don't _connect_ to those networks. It would be very very easy for someone to reproduce if they did reply andrewla 11 hours ago | root | parent | prev | next [–] Agreed that the fact that the capability exists is bad. That said, open networks have become a bit of a rarity; the only ones I can see are captive portal networks, and none of those from my home. reply pixl97 12 hours ago | root | parent | prev | next [–] Wasn't there some issues with TVs in the past that filled up their drives with this data and would then crash or otherwise not work? reply hermitdev 11 hours ago | root | parent | next [–] I have a recent 60ish inch LG OLED that's not been connected to the internet AFAICT for over a year. HDMI-CEC switches aren't KVM switches that only do HDMI. An HDMI-CEC switcher box (or devices with that functionality built into them, like many soundbars) doesn't act as its own isolated sub-HDMI-CEC bus, where the switch presents to its downstreams as the root HDMI-CEC device, catching (without bubbling) <Active Source> messages from said downstreams, selecting one downstream to be active in an internal sense, and then presenting itself to its upstream connected TV or what-have-you as if it's one leaf-node source whose video+audio signals just-so-happen to be those of the currently-selected downstream. Rather, at an HDMI-CEC level, an HDMI switch is a lot more like a USB switch: it passes through all the CEC message broadcasts from all of its downstream source devices through to its upstream receiver device (and vice-versa), sometimes also interpreting them in turn for effect; and the root host device can actually see the whole tree topology, including any switches. (Fun fact: HDMI-CEC devices have four-step hierarchical addresses, that look like IP addresses, describing at each step the physical socket-number offset on the upstream device that connects said upstream to the given downstream. The TV is always 0.0.0.0. Whatever's plugged into the TV's first HDMI socket is 1.0.0.0. If that thing is an HDMI switcher box, then whatever's plugged into its first downstream HDMI socket is 1.1.0.0. And so on. All of these devices can see and talk to one another using these addresses, at all times. It's a network!) Importantly, this means that if a TV is plugged into an HDMI switcher box, which in turn has several source devices plugged into it, then the TV will still be aware of , and can still hear and speak to , all the inactive sources downstream of the switcher box, not just the active one. Which in turn means that if your TV is really stupid in the way it handles HDMI-CEC (e.g. trying to "argue" with sources about who's supposed to be active on wake, with the TV trying to force the last-active source and the source that woke the TV trying to force itself as the active source), then putting an HDMI-CEC switcher box in between will by no means improve things. They'll still be arguing, now "through" the switcher box; and the switcher box will itself be doing additional things in response to seeing these messages. Where previously you had O(N) HDMI-CEC problems, now you'll have O(N log N) HDMI-CEC problems. But hey, at least your leaf-node sources in this tree all show up in the TV's input switcher menu! Disable Stock Launcher and Setup Wizard Run the following commands to disable the default Google TV launcher and the setup wizard (which often reverts changes on reboot): # adb shell pm disable-user --user 0 com.google.android.apps.tv.launcherx # adb shell pm disable-user --user 0 com.google.android.tungsten.setupwraith Note: On some newer TCL models running Android 14, you may need to temporarily disable the package installer (com.android.packageinstaller) to sideload APKs, or manually select the new launcher via the Home button prompt after disabling the stock launcher. 4. In my tests, it seemed like it can be kept offline forever but at the cost of manually dismissing the Wifi config workflow with three clicks on the remote every ~10 power-ons. The TV also will not turn on and just display an external HDMI source even though it has a "Remember Last Source" feature. That feature does work as expected with any internal streaming source but external sources must first be manually selected with the remote after each power on (also undocumented in the manual). I figured this out because I bought this small TV to be a wall-mounted screen in the dedicated bathroom of our home theater room. It's only job is to turn on while someone is in the little bathroom and display a copy what's on the main 150" projector screen in the next room, then turn off when they leave. The on/off is handled by a motion sensor and standard Home Assistant automation but after power on it correctly shows the Last Selected external HDMI source for 1 second, then blanks the screen. The source is already selected and working but being blacked out until you manually re-select the same source with the remote (only if it's external). This is clearly an undocumented anti-pattern added specifically to prevent the TV being used unattended as a display screen, picture frame, digital sign etc. Why? Because Vizio (now owned by WalMart) doesn't get rev share if it's: 1) Not online, and 2) Only displaying external sources. That's why it demands manual "proof-of-life" before it'll grudgingly deliver the basic functionality it claims on the box. This made me angry - and the TV was otherwise the perfect size and feature set for my use case. So I programmed an ESP32 with an IR emitter so that every time the TV powers on it sends the remote presses to manually clear the "Please Connect Internet" message and re-select the already-selected external HDMI. Very annoying to be forced to figure this out but now it works fine and no one even sees the annoying messages as they're already gone before by the time we enter and see the screen. This is why I kept it and spent the time 'fixing' it. Of course, this is only because the TV is subsidized by the $35-$60 avg yearly revenue TV manufacturers reportedly can collect from advertising, app install payments, rev shares and selling all your viewing data. For $88 at local retail, it's probably being sold at a small loss. What's sad is I would have paid double that for the same TV without the dark patterns (in fact, I did buy and return two 24" TVs before this one for $160 and $200 but they couldn't even display external HDR or 24fps sources at all - which was a requirement since this secondary display has to display sources configured for the main projector). reply Mattwmaster58 1 day ago | parent | next [–] lol, I Ctrl+F'ed for this brand after having pointed my agent at it. Transport Ebikes Electric Motorcycles Bus Hyperloop Autonomy Tesla Autopilot Cruise Automation Uber Waymo Energy Green Energy Climate Tesla Shop Store Toggle dark mode BYD BYD sold more EVs last month than the US did all quarter, topping 300,000 Peter Johnson  | Nov 2 2026 - 9:24 am PT 11 Comments BYD sold over 300,000 electric vehicles in October, a new record and more than the US managed in the entire third quarter. BYD October EV sales reach a record 300,000+ The world’s leading EV maker is showing no signs of slowing down. BYD sold 490,168 new energy vehicles (NEVs) in October, up 11% from the prior year and the company’s highest monthly total in 2026. BYD’s battery electric vehicles drove the growth, with a record 305,743 units sold, up 37% year over year and marking the first time its EV sales have crossed the 300,000 mark. To put that into perspective, just over 262,500 EVs were sold in the US in the entire third quarter combined, according to Kelley Blue Book estimates. Advertisement - scroll for more content October marked BYD’s sixth straight month of higher sales growth and its third straight month of higher EV sales. Through October, BYD sold 1,953,700 electric vehicles, up 6% from the same period last year. BYD October 2026 NEV sales (Source: BYD) BYD’s all-electric vehicles (EVs) accounted for about 63% of total sales last month. Plug-in hybrid vehicles, meanwhile, fell 17% in October to 177,382 units. Through October, BYD’s PHEV sales fell 11% to 1,625,969 units. According to BYD’s filing, the company exported 170,194 vehicles in October as it expands overseas to drive growth in markets like Europe, Southeast Asia, and Central and South America. BYD “Xi’an” car carrier loading Dolphin Surf EVs for Europe (Source: BYD) Through October, BYD exported over 1.5 million electric and plug-in hybrid vehicles, nearly double compared to last year. By the end of 2026, BYD expects overseas shipments to reach about 2 million vehicles. In 2027, that number is expected to rise to more than 2.5 million vehicles. BYD opens first Flash Chargers in Germany (Source: Klaus Hartmann/ BYD) Top comment by KingFisher Liked by 7 people For Musk to back the Largest Criminal Government in US History is mystifying. This Pay to Play, the US has never seen the scope of this criminality. What crime did Musk commit? The in your face disrespect for the law, and constitution are shocking. View all comments With several new and updated vehicles launching with its new Blade Battery 2.0 and Flash Charging technology, BYD aims to continue attracting new buyers with longer range, faster charging, and more tech-oriented models. Electrek’s Take While the US is coming off its best quarter of the year in EV sales, BYD’s performance shows how far ahead China is in the transition to electric vehicles. China continues to lead the global EV market, accounting for over half of all electric cars sold worldwide. With a wave of low-cost domestic brands flooding China’s market, BYD and other automakers are driving growth overseas in major markets like Europe, South Korea, Southeast Asia, and Central and South America, where legacy OEMs are already falling behind quickly. title: F/OSS Comics #13: BSD Unix, Part 3 – The Beginning of BSD Unix
body_text: 13. BSD Unix, Part 3 - The Beginning of BSD Unix F/OSS Comics Home All posts About Tags 13. BSD Unix, Part 3 - The Beginning of BSD Unix Posted on Oct 30, 2026 EN KO Display dialogue text Share options ↗ Copy link f Facebook @ Threads B Bluesky X X ••• More sharing options… BSD Unix, Part 1 - Unix Code Goes to UC Berkeley BSD Unix, Part 2 - The Birth of the vi Editor The beginning of BSD Unix When Ken Thompson returned to Bell Labs in 1976, Bill Joy and Chuck Haley began exploring the Unix kernel themselves. Hmm... we could speed things up here in the kernel. Let's try it. Hmm... we could speed things up here in the kernel. Let's try it. Other universities want copies of our Pascal compiler. Let's bundle it with ex and send them a tape. Other universities want copies of our Pascal compiler. Let's bundle it with ex and send them a tape. In early 1977, Bill Joy put together the Berkeley Software Distribution, or BSD, bundling the Pascal system with ex, a line editor developed from em. Early BSD was not a standalone operating system: it was a collection of software to install on an existing Unix system. About thirty copies were sent out over the following year. [1] Thirty tapes to copy... Thirty tapes to copy... At the time, an AT&T Unix source license was needed to get BSD. Berkeley charged only for the tape and distribution. [2] If you already have a Unix source license, it's just the tape and postage. If you already have a Unix source license, it's just the tape and postage. Berkeley already had a tradition of sharing research software. BSD carried it on. Berkeley's Free Speech Movement, hippie culture, and antiwar activism are also said to have influenced Joy's decision to charge so little. [2] Universities and research institutions could obtain Unix, including its source code, for a modest licensing fee. This also helped the system spread. [2] [6] We have Unix, but the antitrust agreement bars us from the computer business... We can't sell it as a product, either. Fluctuations in Power Grids Solved Mystery of 60-Second Fluctuations in Power Grids Solved 30 October 2026 Why do our grids show a brief spike in electricity demand every minute? A team led by Dirk Witthaut from Forschungszentrum Jülich has now demonstrated that this is due to regular power checks carried out by large-scale battery storage systems. These findings could help to make our electricity supply more robust, as the team reports in an article published in Nature Energy . Copyright: Regine Panknin Tennet Germany, the largest transmission system operator in Germany, has observed over several years that the frequency in the European power grid dips briefly every 60 seconds. While these deviations were not critical to grid security, they were clearly measurable and unusually regular. The cause of this phenomenon was initially unclear. A team at Forschungszentrum Jülich led by Dirk Witthaut—who is also a professor at the Institute for Theoretical Physics at the University of Cologne—joined forces with other researchers from the University of Cologne and the Karlsruhe Institute of Technology to search for an answer—and they found it: the cause appears to be the many large-scale battery storage systems that check their state of charge every minute. This leads to measurable fluctuations in electricity consumption, which can contribute to turbine wear and tear, for example. The battery storage systems ensure an uninterrupted power supply, and their numbers have increased significantly worldwide in recent years. The researchers found that this was not a European phenomenon, but a global one. Many devices, a common rhythm “It really was years of detective work,” says Witthaut. The grid frequency pattern is shaped by many different factors. For example, it reveals the influence of electricity trading, with power stations being switched on and off abruptly, as well as the fluctuating feed-in from renewable energy sources, and various other disturbances. Uns war schnell klar, dass es sich bei der Ursache um etwas handeln muss, das von der Uhr gesteuert wird Prof. Dr. Dirk Witthaut, Leiter des Departments Netzwerke und komplexe Systeme, Institut für Energiesystemtechnik (ICE-1) “It quickly became clear to us that the cause must be something controlled by the clock,” says Witthaut. There was no other way to explain the precise 60-second cycle. It was also clear that: “The observed effect can only be produced if many devices are consuming electricity at the same time.” A single consumer or generator could therefore be ruled out. Measurements on campus provide the clue But how do all these devices synchronize their consumption? The researchers finally found the crucial clues with the help of the Living Lab Energy Campus. This research infrastructure on the Jülich campus is primarily used to develop and test highly integrated energy supply systems. The team installed measuring points on end devices at a total of 80 locations – and sure enough, the same periodic pattern in electricity consumption was observed precisely at the locations where large-scale battery storage systems are designed to ensure an uninterrupted power supply. “We took a closer look at one of them and found a spike in electricity consumption at the start of every minute due to the power check,” explains Witthaut. Detektive work from Carsten Hartmann and Dirk Witthaut of the Jülich Institute for Energy systems engineering Copyright: Forschungszentrum Jülich / Dirk Witthaut As there are no binding standards for such power checks, Witthaut suspects that most battery manufacturers assumed that a 60-second interval would be sensible. The start of every minute was simply chosen as the test time. “It is entirely possible, however, that battery storage systems are only part of the problem here,” says Witthaut. “It cannot be ruled out that other digitally controlled appliances – such as air-conditioning systems, heat pumps, washing machines, and dishwashers – may also exhibit similar patterns.” Less synchronization, less wear and tear The periodic fluctuations in electricity demand are already having an impact on hydroelectric power stations. The brief spikes in demand mean that the turbines slow down momentarily before accelerating back to their original rotational speed. This increases wear and tear. With the expansion of storage technologies, such problems could become even more prevalent. In Ireland, for example, where data centres with large-scale battery storage systems currently account for around a fifth of the country’s electricity demand, the amplitude of the 1-minute signal quadrupled between 2016 and 2021. The solution, however, would be simple: “You would simply have to distribute the checks randomly, rather than always starting them at the same time,” says Witthaut. Original publication: 'One-minute frequency disturbances from unintended synchronization in cyber–physical power systems', Nature Energy 2026, DOI: 10.1038/s41560-026-02144-0 Contact Prof. Dr. Dirk Witthaut Head of Department Institute of Climate and Energy Systems (ICE) Energy Systems Engineering (ICE-1) Building 10.21 / Room 4014 +49 2461/61-6178 E-Mail Prof. Andrea Benigni Director Institute of Climate and Energy Systems (ICE) Energy Systems Engineering (ICE-1) Building 10.21 / Room 4011 +49 2461/61-85523 E-Mail Media contact Dr. Regine Panknin Pressereferentin Building 15.3 / Room R 3028 +49 2461/61-9054 E-Mail More on the topic Energy transition Build Up More Energy Reserves With each percent more electricity generated from wind and solar power, it is becoming increasingly clear: more storage is required for the energy transition. In particular, different storage systems are needed – not just different types of batteries, but also hydrogen. This is the only way to offset fluctuations, cope with periods in which little to no energy is generated, and keep the network stable. Energy supply The blackout fairy tale Are nationwide power cuts in Germany due to supply shortages something we have to fear? No, says Jülich grid expert Prof. Dirk Witthaut. He also explains why, in some cases, legal regulations are a much bigger problem for the stability of electricity grids than renewable energies. title: An Italian farmer found some unknown seeds in his attic and planted them
body_text: An Italian Farmer Found Some Unknown Seeds in His Attic and, With Nothing to Lose, Planted Them. The Result Was Almost Biblical Skip to main content Search Shop Newsletters Renew Give a Gift Subscribe Membership i Subscribe Give a Gift Renew Sections Smart News History Science Innovation Arts & Culture Travel At the Smithsonian More from Smithsonian magazine Newsletters Photo Contest Podcast Videos Our Partners Smithsonian Store Smithsonian Journeys Subscribe to Smithsonian magazine and get a FREE tote. An Italian Farmer Found Some Unknown Seeds in His Attic and, With Nothing to Lose, Planted Them. The Result Was Almost Biblical When a seven-eared stem emerged from the ground, it seemed like a miracle. What Claudio Grossi had unearthed was an ancient grain that proved to be an answer to some modern problems Lina Zeldovich Photographs by Clara Vannucci November 2026 Share Copy link Email SMS Facebook X Reddit LinkedIn Bluesky Print Add as preferred source At his farm near Parma, Italy, Claudio Grossi offers a visual history of his miracle grain in photos, crackers and loaves. Clara Vannucci Sometime in the early 1990s, Claudio Grossi, a 40-year-old farmer in Parma, in northern Italy, was cleaning his attic when he turned up an old sack full of seeds that he couldn’t identify. The bag, he was sure, had been left by his late great-grandfather, who’d started the farmstead around 1915. Grossi had no idea how long the seeds had been sitting there, deprived of water, soil and sun. Dry and cracked, the kernels looked so old in the palm of his hand that he doubted anything would ever sprout from them. He carried the bag down the stairs, shook the seeds out into a pile of manure and then forgot about them. To his surprise, the seeds soon sprouted a few different types of wheat. One was particularly striking: At six feet high, its plants were about twice as tall as commercial wheat. But the most remarkable feature came when it developed ears—the grain-studded parts at the top of the plant. All of the wheat types Grossi had previously seen grew only one such ear. But the tall wheat grew a full seven ears, always in the same pattern: a long one with six shorties bunched up around it like little fingers. Even the kernels themselves were bigger than those of average wheat. And unlike the typical pale-yellow wheat kernels, they came in a rainbow of colors—yellow, black, red, white and even green, sometimes all on the same stem. Grossi, a grain farmer his whole life, had never seen anything like it. “I thought it was a freak of nature,” he says. He couldn’t find a mention of it in agricultural books. Ears grown from the very first seeds Grossi discovered in his attic. Grossi prizes these first grains, now preserved under glass in his kitchen. Clara Vannucci Subscribe to Smithsonian magazine now for just $19.99 This article is a selection from the November 2026 issue of Smithsonian magazine Subscribe For Grossi, a practicing Catholic, the next insight came from a different book altogether. Leafing through a Bible at church one Sunday, he found a passage in the Book of Genesis describing a stalk with seven ears, in a dream that Joseph interprets for the Pharaoh: “And he slept and dreamed the second time: And, behold, seven ears of grain came up upon one stalk, rank and good. And, behold, seven thin ears and blasted with the east wind sprung up after them. And the seven thin ears devoured the seven rank and full ears.” To Grossi, that sounded just like the mysterious crop in his manure pile. “I connected the dots,” Grossi says. That grain must be really ancient , he thought. And if people were farming this odd-looking wheat in biblical times, why does no one today? Back on his farm, Grossi harvested the grain, milled it into flour and baked a loaf of bread in his kitchen. Compared with commercial wheat, the dough didn’t rise well, but as the loaf sat in the oven, it filled the kitchen with a surprisingly nutty and delicious aroma. Once finished, it had a rich, satisfying taste. “You get these notes of sweetness that you can’t find in regular commercial flour,” he says. Did you know? More miracles of grain in the Bible In 2 Kings 4:42-44 , Elisha multiplies 20 barley loaves in order to feed 100 men—anticipating Jesus’s “Feeding of the 5,000” in the gospels.  In 1 Kings 17:8-16 , Elisha helps a widow at Zarephath to outlast a drought and famine with only a handful of flour and a little oil.  In Judges 7:9-15 , a Midianite soldier recounts a dream in which a barley loaf tumbles into the camp and overturns a tent. Gideon, the judge and military leader, recognizes the dream as a sign that God will deliver the Midianites into Israel's hands.  In 2 Kings 4:38-41 , during a famine, someone gathers wild gourds and cuts them into a pot of stew. The diners discover that the stew is dangerous and cry out to Elisha. He calls for flour and throws it into the pot—and the stew becomes miraculously safe to eat.  Grossi holds sheaves of his grain, cultivated on the same farm his great-grandfather tilled starting around 1915.  Clara Vannucci Grossi discovered it had other advantages: It was hardier and more self-sufficient than commercial varieties. It fared better during droughts, growing so tall that it overshadowed the weeds. It didn’t need fertilizer or herbicides. Indeed, it seemed so superior to its industrial cousins that he thought of it no longer as a freak of nature but as a wonder. He dubbed it grano del miracolo —“miracle grain” or “miracle wheat.” Grossi’s discovery came at just the right time. In Italy in the 1990s, a burgeoning slow-food movement aimed to preserve traditional farming practices and promote natural diets. Grossi hoped that miracolo could ride this slow-food wave, becoming both a portal to the past and a passage to a future. Perhaps, he thought, miracolo could help other farmers bring back ancient grains, leading the movement that is changing how we make bread, a staple of the human diet. And today, as climate change makes droughts, heat waves and plant disease outbreaks more frequent and intense, a grain that has shown it can fend for itself would help keep that bread on the table. Farmers began cultivating wheat about 10,000 years ago, in the Fertile Crescent —the area of the Middle East known as the Cradle of Civilization. Thousands of years ago, the hardy and adaptable plant took hold in Europe and Asia. Compared with our modern crops, these ancient wheats were much taller, outperforming other grasses in the field. Over the millennia, humans bred different varieties of wheat, some yielding less grain and others more. As human populations grew, the strains of wheat that brought plentiful harvests became more desirable. That pattern accelerated amid the upheavals of the early 20th century. By the early 1920s, Italy was still recovering from World War I and unable to grow enough grain to sustain itself; the country was importing roughly a third of its wheat. When fascist leader Benito Mussolini became prime minister in 1922, he launched a campaign to “free the Italian people from the slavery of foreign bread,” by pushing for wheat varieties that yielded greater harvests. The Italian government promoted and planted these “elite” varieties, then distributed the seeds to farmers. Named la Battaglia del Grano , or the Battle of Wheat, this campaign became a global model for agrarian development. In the United States, wheat harvests were then still plentiful, but not for long: By the early 1930s, amid unprecedented droughts, American farmers found the land was exhausted. The result was the Dust Bowl , during which the previously fertile soils of the Great Plains turned into a desert. American farmers had to look for more drought-resistant varieties that still yielded enough grain. The midcentury Green Revolution, a movement launched by the American agronomist Norman Borlaug , focused on selective breeding and boosted crop production. This work spread worldwide, feeding countless people. The wheat that was created was indeed more plentiful, yet it came with trade-offs. The petite plants couldn’t always outcompete weeds and were susceptible to disease, so growers used weed killers, fungicides and fertilizer to sustain the crops. Little did they know that these practices would only weaken the health of the soil—while making the wheat even less resilient to changing climate and extreme weather events. In the 1990s, Grossi sensed that anxiety over wheat harvests was building. That’s why, after he grew wheat from those seeds in the attic, he set out to put the hardy ancient grain back on the table. First, he realized he’d have to solve a big problem: Bread made from the wheat leavened poorly, rising only to fall again. In the early 2000s, he began discussing this challenge with an old local baker who shunned modern machines and still kneaded his dough by hand. The baker was intrigued. The two men started experimenting. They tried letting the dough rise in smaller batches, using wicker baskets that were taller and helped the dough keep its shape. Soon, the two found another secret: Less kneading made miracolo leaven even better. “The dough was rising, and it was holding its shape,” Grossi says. One new fan of the bread was Beniamino Perobelli , a student in food science at the University of Parma, who tasted the miracolo bread at a local farmers market and dedicated his undergraduate thesis to investigating its nutritional value. That work bore out what Grossi had already intuited: This wheat was truly ancient—and truly special. Working with the lab of Teofilo Vamerali , then a professor at the University of Parma, Perobelli determined that the grain was Triticum turgidum —literally “swollen wheat” in Latin. Known in English as “poulard wheat,” it had originally evolved in what today are Turkey, Egypt and other nearby Mediterranean countries. And searching agricultural references, Perobelli found that it had been grown in Italy, too, until farmers shifted toward higher-yield commercial varieties. That solved the mystery of the seed bag stashed away in the attic: It had survived because Grossi’s grandfather saved some of the heritage grains. The food scientists found that, compared with modern wheats, grano del miracolo was richer in phosphorus and iron. Moreover, to their surprise, they found that T. turgidum had less gluten than modern wheat. And it packed a lot of lysine and tryptophan, the essential amino acids that serve as proteins’ building blocks. It also had more arginine, an amino acid that children need to grow. “The richness of microelements, minerals, and the greater presence of proteins other than gluten were very pleasant surprises,” says Perobelli, now a corporate social responsibility and sustainability manager with Rigoni di Asiago , an Italian company that produces organic fruit spreads, honey and more. Grossi displays a bag of barley coffee, made with heirloom plants grown on his farm. This  barley is known as “Leonessa,” or “lioness.”  Clara Vannucci For Grossi, Perobelli’s findings offered scientific proof of his grain’s goodness. He persuaded Molino Grassi , a local organic grain company, to offer the flour to artisanal bakers. Over the next few years, Grossi upped production, so Molino Grassi could sell the flour to restaurants and consumers in Italy and abroad. By the 2010s, traditional recipes were enjoying a renaissance. So were artisanal bakers and pasta makers, who also became more discerning about which grains they used, says Francesco Sottile , an expert in biodiversity of agrosystems at the University of Palermo. Ancient grains aren’t necessarily perfect. For example, Grossi has found that miracolo’s height can be a liability—which may be why it fell out of favor with Mussolini. Heavy winds, rains and hail can make the tall stems flip over before the grain ripens, ruining harvests. But Grossi circumvented the problem by planting miracolo with shorter wheat varieties that provide structural support. “I’m quite happy because I developed something that’s like a discovery,” he says. Relying on a limited number of wheat cultivars, Sottile argues, leaves humanity vulnerable to agricultural disasters: prolonged droughts, extreme heat, new diseases or pests that develop resistance to our chemicals. Diversifying grains reduces the risk—even if some varieties succumb to environmental pressures, others will stand. Sottile shared an example. “I’m based in Sicily,” he says, where 2024 saw “one of the worst droughts in the last 35 to 40 years.” It was so bad that many commercial wheat growers abandoned their fields in April of that year, realizing they wouldn’t be able to reap the seeds they sowed. Sottile was heartened to see a better fate among smaller-batch farmers who grew heritage grains, more resilient to extreme weather. “Most of the farmers who were adopting ancient grains, they were able to collect, to harvest,” Sottile says. The world needs more crop biodiversity, he adds—including more ancient grains like grano del miracolo. By the same token, we need more people like Grossi, who, much like the ancient grain he sows, have the tenacity to make a miracle happen. Stories of gods and grains “Miracle wheat” is hardly the first divine cereal. Across millennia, gods have taught mortals how to earn their bread By Sonja Anderson Louvre Museum / Public Domain Greece: While Dionysus provided grapes and Athena was responsible for olives, the goddess Demeter brought grain to the Greeks. In myth, the latter goddess taught farming to a man named Triptolemus (pictured at right), then sent him out on a winged chariot to deliver the knowledge to all of Greece—an episode immortalized on ancient vases. Mesopotamia: Ancient Sumerians of the Fertile Crescent attributed farming to Ashnan, the grain goddess, “whose face is honey-covered / The lady, the procreatress, the vigor of the land,” per an ancient Sumerian poem. In myth, Ashnan and her sibling Lahar, deity of livestock, once drunkenly debated whether grains or sheep were more important. Enlil and Enki, the paramount Sumerian gods, declared Ashnan the winner, saying that without grain—often fed to herds—there could be no sheep. Egypt: Osiris ruled over death and the afterlife but was also a god of fertility, and it was said he taught mankind to cultivate wheat. Ancient Egyptians became famously adept at managing this crop: Their growing seasons regularly produced surpluses, thanks to the Nile’s floods. Some priests honored Osiris by planting grain in earthenware shaped like the god. China: Some ancient Chinese myths trace the country’s agriculture back to one emperor of legend: Shennong , born of a princess and a dragon some 4,000 years ago. The ruler supposedly had a bull’s head and a man’s body and is known as the divine farmer, or emperor of five grains (including rice, millets and wheat). He taught his people how to till their land, expanding the ancient Chinese diet—consisting mainly of meat, clams and wild fruits—to include grains and vegetables. Mexico: Quetzalcoatl was a deity of the Aztec civilization who, according to myth, created the humans of our current era—the Fifth Sun—and their world. He taught people how to carve rocks, dye cotton, read the stars and—most important—grow food. One day, Quetzalcoatl observed a black ant carrying a kernel of corn, turned himself into an ant and followed the insect through a crack in a stone mountain, where he found a trove of maize, beans, peppers and sage. He took a corn kernel, brought it to man and taught him how to plant it. title: Mathematics has changed. Let's act like it
body_text: Mathematics has changed. Let’s act like it | What's new What's new Updates on my research and expository papers, discussion of open problems, and other maths-related topics. By Terence Tao Home About Career advice On writing Books Mastodon+ Applets Subscribe to feed Mathematics has changed. Let’s act like it 1 November, 2026 in guest blog , opinion | Tags: Frank Calegari | by Terence Tao [This is a guest post by Frank Calegari . This blog post was initially written in a different file format and converted using AI. — T.] Why we should not be sad The release by OpenAI on October 6 of over 700 research papers was a watershed in the history of mathematics. AI is now undeniably capable of making groundbreaking contributions across many areas of mathematics. So why are some mathematicians so unhappy? Some of it is the apparent disregard by AI companies for the practice of mathematics. The OpenAI papers — despite some tremendous ideas — are atrociously written and violate our community expectations of attribution. Some of them are even wrong. We have much more control over how we hire mathematicians, publish papers, and train students than over the behavior of trillion-dollar companies, and that is where our efforts would be better spent. Much of the reaction seems to reflect a feeling that the subject that they love is under attack, and is being “hollowed out”. The recent OpenAI dump made barely a dent on the general problems of functoriality and reciprocity in the Langlands program. But even if it had solved every problem in the Langlands program, to imagine that would have “solved number theory” would be as naive as saying that the construction of the periodic table solved chemistry. Mathematicians should do a better job explaining that when we talk about the central problems in any area, we are merely discussing the most natural boundaries of our understanding — and that unlocking them is not the end but the first step to finding new playgrounds to explore. Of course, this takes time. I looked for areas of mathematics which were “harder hit”. It is hard not to be struck by Hugo Duminil-Copin’s lament : Not a single one of the major open problems I have publicly mentioned throughout my career (whether in a talk, a lecture, an article, or even a grant proposal) was left untouched by the announcement. Everything has been claimed to be proved. I expected to see a few of them in the list. But not all of them. Not all at once. Not with such nonchalance. How would I respond to that? The classification of finite simple groups. I can’t say much about percolation theory, but there is another historical precedent I think mathematicians should take note of. In 1972, Dan Gorenstein announced a program towards the classification of finite simple groups. After a flurry of activity over around a decade, the “classification” was announced by Gorenstein in 1983 (somewhat prematurely, with the case of quasithin groups not being completed for another two decades by Aschbacher and Smith). The classification of finite simple groups was in many ways a huge success, but it was also a failure in that it — apologies to my group theorist friends and collaborators — cooled a lot of the interest around the subject. The “famous problem” had gone, and mathematicians on the whole turned their attention elsewhere. And yet, there remain very rich questions in finite group theory and even about the classification itself (to name just one: John Conway’s favorite question is why does the Monster group exist? ). Perhaps for some fields, the OpenAI dump feels like how a group theorist may have felt in 1970 if the classification was dumped in their office, not in the form of the actual papers, but printed out on a spirit duplicator, smudged a little, then spread randomly like confetti all over the floor. Right now, we need efforts like that of Gorenstein, Lyons, and Solomon and their work on the revised classification. If this was all we had to do, then it would be a fairly thankless task. But we also have the responsibility not to pronounce the subject “done” but rather — with these new tools available — ripe for further investigation. When mathematicians lament the winding paths missed by the construction of a galactic bypass, they need to realize that those old paths still exist and seek them out. And we need to reward that behavior when it comes to offering people jobs. The promise of AI, and the (dis)-unity of mathematics: Since I was 15, I’ve wanted to know what was. First, there was the childhood fantasy of finding a formula that Euler missed. But soon one learns more: how Grothendieck’s period conjecture, together with a sufficiently fine understanding of the geometry of mixed Tate motives (following work of Don Zagier, Sasha Goncharov, Francis Brown, and others) gives a completely satisfying structural, conjectural explanation of what’s going on. The irrationality of , or even its transcendence, is a mere shadow of the actual interesting underlying problem. Apéry’s proof of the irrationality of has inspired me for over years not because of its conclusion, but for how it reveals the tiniest hints of some still secret story relating algebraic -functions to arithmetic. I hope AI can help mathematicians break out of the straitjacket of being constrained by the first natural conjecture they cannot prove, and work on unraveling the deeper mysteries woven throughout our subject. In the last thirty years, progress in mathematics by humans has been remarkable. But at the same time, I have felt a growing unease; the number of times I have seen mathematicians of all levels being unable to explain to someone even slightly outside their field why what they are doing is interesting has been distressing. The natural grooves of our profession have very much been bent toward more narrow technical expertise than a bigger vision. AI allows us an amazing opportunity to broaden ourselves as mathematicians. I have tried (not always successfully) to be broad as a mathematician. I had some help by the fact that, while I knew since I was 17 that I wanted to work in algebraic number theory and the Langlands program, I grew up in the crucible of Melbourne University, which was a home to many Thurston students and low-dimensional topologists. This meant I was bathed in the sweet liqueur of hyperbolic 3-manifolds. That exposure has helped my career immeasurably. As with any two deep areas of mathematics, hyperbolic three-manifolds and arithmetic are much more closely connected than would first appear. But it’s still hard to be an expert on both, let alone pursue a crazy idea combining them. Let me get technical for a moment. For every imaginary quadratic field , there are many commensurability classes of compact arithmetic hyperbolic three-manifolds indexed by non-split quaternion algebras . Manifolds in each of these commensurability classes give rise to elements in via the decomposition of into hyperbolic tetrahedra, and their volumes are always rational multiples of . I have always had this idea that one could conceive of elements in these different commensurability classes as forming some type of geometric Kolyvagin system (“Heegner points”) associated to , which one could yoke together by some unknown integral arithmetic version of the Jacquet–Langlands correspondence. This is not a question I have pursued, for two reasons. First, there were so many underlying conjectures involved that any result I could prove was going to be conditional on many of them, something that’s not always appreciated by the mathematical community. Second, assembling all the technical background to formulate such an idea precisely would have taken a huge amount of background work. Now, with AI, the barriers to trying such a problem are much lower. It’s not trying to prove a theorem. It’s trying to explore some completely new direction that may or may not be nonsense. There are so many problems in mathematics that are still so fresh and vital but were previously untouchable that the opportunity to approach them is massively exciting. We need to be more ambitious, to create bold research plans that weren’t even conceivable a year ago. This is not to say that everyone must (or must not) use AI. But we have to rethink and readjust what’s important. Proofs of major conjectures, using AI or otherwise, are going to remain part of the new mathematics. But working toward broader programs (new and old) and structural understanding is going to play a more fundamental role. Christian Szegedy raised the following point: Mathematics prided itself on being meritocratic, with deep reverence for the explorers: the people who could climb what nobody else could. That specific kind of heroism will matter less, and other skills will matter more: choosing which terrain is worth exploring, steering fleets of airplanes, and explaining what they find to the rest of the world. I’m ready to board the plane, because I want to see what’s there. At the same time, I would add that people who previously have been walking around on earth with their eyes closed are not going to recognize anything however high they fly; I still believe that many of the skills that mathematicians have now will not only be transferable but vital to the new world order. The difference in reaction between the optimists and the pessimists is that, for the pessimists, the game is over. For the optimists, the game has just changed. I acknowledge that there are aspects of our mathematical culture that we treasure that won’t survive, and it is only human to grieve that loss. But there now exists an amazing new tool to study mathematics. To turn away and say that the community of mathematics as it currently exists is more important than mathematics itself would be a terrible mistake. The ugly truth. For all that everyone has been saying on this blog and elsewhere about how mathematics is about understanding, it takes one look at the arXiv to see many people in our profession rushing out AI-assisted papers in a somewhat unsightly rush to be the “first” to prove things. As many others have noted, there is quickly becoming a gulf between the ability to produce novel proofs and the ability to either demonstrate understanding or push the subject in new and interesting directions. As people crank out more and more results, the Leiden declaration is being honored more in name than in spirit, and it seems like “business as usual” except with a much more compressed time scale and the constant threat of being scooped hanging over people’s heads. To me, someone who chooses a worthwhile problem, obtains a proof completely using AI, understands it thoroughly, and uses it to develop interesting further questions or directions has made a substantial mathematical contribution. I would give that person substantial credit even if they supplied no new ingredient in the original proof. Choosing worthwhile problems may end up mattering more than producing proofs. Our obsession with conjectures tends to greatly undervalue the exploratory work that makes answering (or even asking) these problems possible. We are in danger of making that mistake a hundredfold now by encouraging or rewarding the rush for everyone to press the button to get these new results out as soon as possible. I would encourage all senior mathematicians (with the privilege of tenure) to take up the work of creating future problems and exploring new ideas rather than simply using AI to answer existing questions. If you, as a senior mathematician, are stressed about being scooped by AI, then you are not being ambitious enough. So what are we actually going to do? Think pieces are ultimately pointless unless they propose some mechanism for actually affecting how people act. The tools that are going to be the most effective are going to be economic rather than rhetorical. Mathematicians want recognition, mathematicians want jobs, mathematicians want grants. The tools that we currently have to affect this are hiring and accepting papers at journals. Let me offer some very basic concrete suggestions, followed by a few details. Evaluate all work as if it is AI-assisted. Make hiring much more about personal interactions rather than a paper file. Interview postdocs and graduate students in person. Demand more from journals, and abandon those that do not adapt. Put a greater emphasis on breadth in graduate education, but do not abandon technical skills. Give better seminars. Take more ownership of the results of AI. Evaluations: Nelson Cole famously spent three years of Sundays discovering the prime factorization In , this was a contribution to mathematics. Factoring the same number in by hand would be an equally impressive feat of arithmetic, but its contribution to mathematics (even if it had not previously been known) would be far less, since this can be done on a computer algebra system in far less than a second. It’s obvious that AI is changing the economics of what is “easy” or “hard” — much has already been said about the coming collapse of the theorem economy. In time (perhaps quickly) there will emerge a new sense of what remains a substantial contribution to mathematics, whether it be asking interesting questions, developing new programs, or something completely different. In the future, I see no reason to reward a paper based purely on a result that could be produced by machine, whether it was or not. A new proof can still deserve substantial credit for the ideas it introduces, even when its conclusion is already obtainable by machine. So why not start now? Importantly, I do not think this in any way means that access to AI will be required to make progress in mathematics — as long as we continue to value human understanding. While I feel that this is the most controversial recommendation, I also feel it is the most inevitable. It requires relinquishing an aspect of our reward structure that has been around for a long time, but at the same time a structure that will make no sense in the future. Right now, the use of AI carries a stigma, and the phrasing of many AI disclosures reads more like an attempt to minimize the contribution of the machine. If we evaluate every paper as potentially AI-assisted, then we must insist that its authors explain why the mathematics is interesting, what questions it raises, and how it connects to the broader subject. Don’t we want people to be doing this anyway? Hiring: It’s not going to be possible to get people to change unless we change how we evaluate people at the level of hiring. Lazy committees in the past have sometimes pointed toward a JAMS paper, an Annals paper, or some other collection of publications to justify how a candidate is impressive. I am looking for a narrative of where you want mathematics to go, the technical ability to explain why this may be possible, being able to converse about many areas of mathematics, and a demonstrable record of having done all of this in the past. This is not in any way a radical new idea. The hiring process is going to have to be much more about personal interactions than a paper file. It should become standard practice to interview not only for tenure-track jobs, but also for postdocs and graduate student positions. I’m sure we have all had the experience of admitting a graduate student who was “working on higher homotopy theory” to only find out after they are admitted they can’t compute the homology of the circle. At the same time, I have interviewed candidates at the tenure level whom I was initially ambivalent about, but after a 30 minute conversation in my office I was totally convinced that here was someone who not only had a deep vision of mathematics but who was also able to communicate this to their colleagues. Once we take this approach, we then have the responsibility to train our own graduate students to be better able to communicate mathematics, something that we should take much more seriously. Note there is also a difference between knowing mathematics deeply and explaining it fluently; they are related but different skills. Ideally I want both, but it is the first that I ultimately value more highly. Journals: The journal system was in dire need of reform even before AI. Our current incentives already are to produce more and more incremental mathematics which is only flooding the system. The radical overhaul required is not going to happen through consensus agreements with editorial boards. (Do you know how hard it is to get academics to agree on anything?) Being accepted by a journal has long since ceased to be a guarantee of correctness (if it ever was) and has simply acted as an imprimatur of quality. I explained above the philosophy of how I think we should evaluate manuscripts going forward. On that basis, I would say that a significant proportion of papers posted to the arXiv should not be published anywhere. If journals demand much more from a paper in terms of writing, ideas, and exposition, I think that would make life better for everyone — editors, reviewers, and even ultimately authors. If editorial boards are unable to adjust, then a more radical idea is to (at least temporarily) abandon journals altogether. (I still see a place for journals which emphasize exceptional utility and clarity (consider Essential Number Theory )). I am not advocating that people stop writing papers, but removing the fig leaf of journal publication forces the paper to stand on its own merits. Is the paper telling a compelling story? Is it Lean-verified? We should be producing fewer (and better) papers, not more. Autonomously AI-produced proofs, hopefully Lean-checked, also have their place, and should be recorded as part of our collective body of knowledge. (see hexagonmath .) Graduate students, first-year courses, and seminars. One of the thorniest issues we face is how to train graduate students. The typical thesis has always been to assign a problem in the overhang, an exercise that will teach the student the technical skills to solve a variation on some old problem, with the expectation that, as they continue, they can expand the techniques they’ve learned to new cases and then hopefully branch out to wider problems. In an age where such a thesis can be produced by the press of a button, we need to re-evaluate based on what we hope a good student will be doing in the future. Even with AI resources, no one is going to be able to explore the links between compact arithmetic hyperbolic three-manifolds and Kolyvagin systems if they don’t know what either of these terms means. (And even if somehow they could, why would they care?) It has become much more important to give students a broader overview of mathematics as a discipline. What I want a graduate student to achieve at the end of their PhD is a view of mathematics that extends well beyond their discipline, and yet with demonstrable technical skills on at least some class of problems. Often, students graduate with technical skills in a subarea, but their experience with other aspects of their area, let alone other areas of mathematics, consists of technical instruction which they have since forgotten, without any real vision. I advocated above that we need to evaluate work as if AI was involved. But this does not imply that we don’t need to teach students to do deep mathematics without AI just as the existence of computers doesn’t mean we should no longer teach children arithmetic. This has consequences for what we teach, as well as how students learn to talk about it. A graduate course should leave students with some understanding of what the topic makes possible elsewhere in mathematics. We should expect them to retain a sense of the questions and connections, even when they have forgotten some of the technical details. If we are to evaluate people more on how they can demonstrate understanding in person, we clearly need to be far more conscious of training our students to explain mathematics to other people, either in person, or in seminars, and to their peers. We need to work on giving our students opportunities to learn this skill. Remember that the most successful cohorts of students are the ones who learn together and who talk mathematics with each other. We should also not forget that not everyone who completes a PhD in mathematics goes on to academia. We should also ask whether the length and structure of doctoral training serve students who will pursue careers outside academia. Seminars: Seminars are traditionally where someone presents the details of their latest result. Because math is difficult, this almost always consists of explaining some minor tweak to a previous method, often without anywhere near enough broader context to make it interesting. Instead, seminars should rarely be focused entirely on new work. They should be framed around the broader interesting questions, explaining the avenues on which we are stuck, on which we can make progress, on which we are hopeful, and then perhaps at the very end explaining some novelty, if there is any. This is how I have always encouraged my students to give talks! As senior faculty we all need to be vocal in our seminars demanding more from our speakers. Ownership. Mathematicians as a profession would do well to take more ownership of these results. What has come out of the machine has been built on the intellectual foundations of several millennia of human mathematical endeavor. Once you start to take credit on behalf of humanity (rather than attributing these results to either a Silicon Valley tycoon or a mathematical Twitter buffoon), you’ll immediately start to feel much better. The world is looking at us. My dean recently visited New York to meet with donors and other friends of the University of Chicago, and everyone she spoke to, regardless of whether they were a math major or not, wanted to talk to her about mathematics. The world is looking at us. There are many many people who care about mathematics without necessarily having a deep technical background ( 3Blue1Brown has over six million subscribers!). All of my friends in the humanities truly believe that having mathematicians in society both as custodians of one of humanity’s oldest intellectual activities and explorers of the frontiers of knowledge is important. I understand that some part of the culture we so deeply care about will disappear, and as humans, an emotional response to that is very natural. But this is a time to explain to everyone that there are so many great new opportunities, possibilities, and reasons to be optimistic. We are on the verge of a new era of mathematics, and I am excited to see what happens. Notes: For more context on Duminil-Copin’s remarks, see also this numberphile video . His full quote also says “We are a resilient community, and I have no doubt that we will adapt”. Many of the themes mentioned here have been brought up in other posts. To give three examples: The idea that mathematicians should take more ownership of the results produced by AI was also explored in Nestor Guillen’s post . The idea that AI gives us the opportunity to be far more ambitious is raised in Ben Antieau’s post . The idea that we need to revisit our reward structure to create the right incentives was explored in Bryna Kra’s post. title: Leaking Secrets from Air-Gap Computers by Spelling Radio Signals from RAM (2024)
body_text: [2409.02292] RAMBO: Leaking Secrets from Air-Gap Computers by Spelling Covert Radio Signals from Computer RAM Skip to main content Search Submit Donate Log in Search arXiv Press Enter to search · Advanced search --> Computer Science > Cryptography and Security arXiv:2409.02292 (cs) [Submitted on 3 Sep 2024] Title: RAMBO: Leaking Secrets from Air-Gap Computers by Spelling Covert Radio Signals from Computer RAM Authors: Mordechai Guri View a PDF of the paper titled RAMBO: Leaking Secrets from Air-Gap Computers by Spelling Covert Radio Signals from Computer RAM, by Mordechai Guri View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Air-gapped systems are physically separated from external networks, including the Internet. This isolation is achieved by keeping the air-gap computers disconnected from wired or wireless networks, preventing direct or remote communication with other devices or networks. Air-gap measures may be used in sensitive environments where security and isolation are critical to prevent private and confidential information leakage. In this paper, we present an attack allowing adversaries to leak information from air-gapped computers. We show that malware on a compromised computer can generate radio signals from memory buses (RAM). Using software-generated radio signals, malware can encode sensitive information such as files, images, keylogging, biometric information, and encryption keys. With software-defined radio (SDR) hardware, and a simple off-the-shelf antenna, an attacker can intercept transmitted raw radio signals from a distance. The signals can then be decoded and translated back into binary information. We discuss the design and implementation and present related work and evaluation results. This paper presents fast modification methods to leak data from air-gapped computers at 1000 bits per second. Finally, we propose countermeasures to mitigate this out-of-band air-gap threat. Running a bootstrapped SaaS for 20 years with my brother
body_text: 20 years. 766 million files. Two Chameleons. - The Zamzar Blog Skip to content Close Menu Search for: Search The Zamzar Blog Free Your Files Menu 20 years. 766 million files. Two Chameleons. by The Zamzar Team October 30, 2026 October 30, 2026 In 2006, two brothers launched a website using dial-up modems and a battered book on writing HTML4, named it after a character who woke up as a giant insect , and hoped someone might find it useful. Twenty years and 766,615,348 file conversions later, apparently someone did. Some Ridiculous Numbers Back when we launched Zamzar in 2006 we proudly offered a whopping 150 different conversion types. We now offer almost 15x that 👀, with 2,128 conversions supported in 2026. Over 550 million people have used Zamzar since launch, converting over 766 million files . We now process over 1 million API requests per day. Big numbers are great (they keep our resident stats-man Mike happy) but more important than features and numbers are the people that find and use Zamzar every day. Last year alone, we had: One visitor from the remote pacific island of Tokelau – with a population of 1,499 it is the fourth smallest sovereign state in the world. Three from Svalbard – a remote Norwegian archipelago which bans cats and has more snowmobiles than people. 38 from Antarctica 🥶 – 🙌 to the 1,000 scientists who stay there over Winter (hope the vending machines are well stocked). 41 from the Vatican – h.t. to Leo 🕍 🕊️ 🙏 We have questions … Twenty years of unexpected adventures It turns out that running a file conversion website can lead you to some pretty strange places. We’ve helped the inventor of PowerPoint recover long-lost presentations ( yes, really ), supported internet pioneer Vint Cerf in his efforts to preserve our digital history, and partnered with Xerox to help their printers turn documents into spoken word audio. We’ve been asked to convert sewing machine patterns (we couldn’t), resurrect ancient eFax files ( we could ), and solve more obscure file format mysteries than we ever imagined existed. Along the way, we’ve appeared on the BBC’s Click , received a cease-and-desist letter from Google for letting people download YouTube videos, and somehow ended up sponsoring a team of Scottish curling champions . That last one definitely wasn’t in the original business plan. Still small, still independent Twenty years on, we’re still a small, proudly independent UK company. No venture capital, no unicorn valuations, and no plans to pivot to an AI-powered blockchain for converting your Gran’s Word documents. We’ve watched countless technology trends come and go – social media, Web 2.0, smartphones, blockchain, wearable tech, NFT’s, the metaverse and more recently the arrival of Al Pacino , sorry AI.. Throughout it all people still need to convert their files. Being independent has also given us the freedom to do things our own way. We’ve supported more than 60 charities, schools and good causes, donating a portion of our profits to organisations doing far more important work than converting PDFs. The people behind the files Behind every one of these 766 million files is a real person with a real problem. Like Robin, who thought 36 pages of work had been lost to “gibberish”, until Zamzar brought them back to life. Or Simha, who discovered Zamzar through a friend in Israel more than a decade ago, and still uses us today from Mexico. It’s stories like these that remind us why we started – making someone’s day a little easier, one file at a time. THANKYOU! Mike and I have loved building and running Zamzar for the last 20 years, but we couldn’t have done it without an amazing team along the way – Suz, Nick, Louis, Grace, Mike, Anna, Sarah and Kate thanks for all you have done. And thanks also to our many, many customers who have sent us notes of encouragement over the years – we read them all and we ❤️ you all 🙂 We built Zamzar because we had files we couldn’t open, and didn’t want to download a program, requiring a CS degree to use it. It turns out 550 million other people had much the same problem. Anyway, somewhere out there is a file that won’t open. We’d better get back to work … Happy Converting, Chris & Mike Whyley, Co-Founders @ Zamzar.
