title: It's the memory latency, stupid
body_text: It's the memory latency, stupid Â· Pivot blog Docs Blog Slack GitHub Get started â All posts It's the memory latency, stupid Making GROUP BY faster by doing more (CPU!) work October 28, 2026 Â· Maor Kern Disclaimer no LLMs were harmed (or for that matter used) in the writing of this blog post When you see your databases CPU at 100%, what is it actually doing? We like to act as though CPUs run code linearly for simplicity's sake, but in truth CPUs are incredibly complex beasts; they can potentially do many instructions at once, or sometimes none at all (despite our console showing 100%). Because CPUs can do so many things, one CPU at 100% may be doing much less than another at 100%. A CPU is considered "idle" only if no task (Linux task) needs CPU time; this does not mean the CPU itself is being fully saturated. So why would a CPU not be fully utilized, even if it appears to be at 100%? The answer is usually memory . Memory accesses are orders of magnitude slower than internal CPU operations. To give a good picture of how much so, a modern CPU might be able to process somewhere in the realm of 4-8 instructions per nanosecond. A memory access to RAM can take somewhere in the realm of 50-100ns. To ease your mathing, that means a modern CPU can do around 400-800 instructions for every one memory access from RAM. CPU CPU core 4â8 instr / ns L1 cache ~1 ns ~64 KB Â· ~4â8 instructions per access L2 cache ~3â4 ns ~1 MB Â· ~15â30 instructions per access L3 cache ~10â15 ns up to a few hundred MB Â· ~50â100 instructions per access DRAM ~50â100 ns GBs Â· ~400â800 instructions per access Given this, CPUs are built from the ground up to work their way around this. The most obvious way this is dealt with is CPU caches. CPU caches keep memory closer to the CPU than RAM, literally baked into the CPU chip. The closest cache (the L1 cache) takes around 1ns per memory operation- that's 50-100x faster than RAM! The "problem" here of course is that the CPU caches are fairly small; the L1 cache for a modern CPU is probably around ~64KB, while the farther caches max out at a few hundred MB for top end processors. A good database tries manipulating data in small "chunks" to take full advantage of caches, and you'll often hear cache utilization as being one of the top concerns of performance engineering. Let's look at GROUP BY aggregations to get a better grip on cache utilization. In GROUP BY, we're looking to take a dataset, group it by a certain column (or more), and perform certain aggregations (for example, count, or sum on another column). The "naive" method might be to open a HashTable keyed by the group key that grows ever larger. For every new row, you would check if that key exists- if it does, go to it's corresponding aggregation and update the result. Simple, right? The problem is that if you have millions of unique groups, you're not utilizing your cache at all! Nearly every HashTable access will be a "cold" hit that goes to RAM. This means that although your CPU may /look/ like it's 100% utilized, in truth it'll constantly be waiting for cold memory accesses. To demonstrate this, we'll take our state-of-the-art Pivot engine and ravage it! We'll remove all our complex logic and replace it with simplicity: fn consume ( & mut self , batch: RecordBatch , _sender: & mut dyn Sender < RecordBatch >, ) -> unary:: Result <()> { let group_keys = batch. column ( self .key_column). as_primitive ::< Int64Type >(); for &key in group_keys. values () { // If the Group Key doesn't exist- set it to 0 // Afterwards, add 1 to the group- this will give us a count(*) GROUP BY key_column * self .counts. entry (key). or_insert ( 0 ) += 1 ; } } We'll then run a simple query SELECT count(*), UserID FROM hits GROUP BY UserID on the "hits" dataset ClickBench provides (99m rows). This query will give us a count per UserID , meaning we'll have an entry in our HashMap per UserID - I'll give a spoiler here that there are ~17m unique UserID . Our performance checks will be on a bare metal server from our good friends over at CherryServers (AMD EPYC 9124 Genoa, 16 cores, 128 GB DDR5). We unfortunately can't use a common AWS/GCP machine because we want access to counters that aren't exposed there for security reasons (for example, we want to see how much memory is passing from DRAM controller to us). We'll confine ourselves to a single core, since this naive group by can't run on many cores. To run it: cat > config.yaml << 'EOF' server : bind : 127.0.0.1:5440 workers : 1 datastores : default : kind : pivotlake location : ./data default : true users : pivot : auth : method : trust EOF taskset -c 3 pivot server --config config.yaml & taskset -c 7 psql -h 127.0.0.1 -p 5440 -U pivot -c '\timing on' -c "SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT COUNT(*), UserID FROM hits GROUP BY UserID)" This takes... a whopping 3.9 seconds. Is that good? Is that bad? Everything in this world is relative, or so they say. If we run the query again (without restarting the server), it takes 3.6s. The second run is the one we're more interested in- there's no disk involved as everything is already sitting in our page-cache. You'll notice we did taskset -c . This pins the process to a given CPU; this will allow us to run perf stat on that CPU and see what's going on internally. We'll measure two metric groups- percentage of CPU slots stalling because of memory (and not doing anything in the meanwhile), and percentage of CPU slots actually retiring a micro-op: sudo perf stat -C 3 -M backend_bound_memory,retiring -- taskset -c 7 psql -h 127.0.0.1 -p 5440 -U pivot -c "SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT COUNT(*), UserID FROM hits GROUP BY UserID)" and we get back this Performance counter stats for 'CPU(s) 3': 8364109137 ex_no_retire.load_not_complete # 50.1 % backend_bound_memory 38233214040 de_no_dispatch_per_slot.backend_stalls 8977647849 ex_no_retire.not_complete 11861387798 ls_not_halted_cyc 11431618219 ex_ret_ops # 16.1 % retiring 11858248045 ls_not_halted_cyc 4.030148989 seconds time elapsed This tells us that 50.1% of the time, the CPU couldn't do anything because it was stalling on memory! And only 16.1% of the time the CPU was actually retiring (aka doing) operations. Another interesting stat to get is how many of our CPU memory loads are coming from DRAM (and not from caches): sudo perf stat -C 3 -e ls_dmnd_fills_from_sys.dram_io_near -- taskset -c 7 psql -h 127.0.0.1 -p 5440 -U pivot -c "SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT COUNT(*), UserID FROM hits GROUP BY UserID)" And the result: Performance counter stats for 'CPU(s) 3': 76190837 ls_dmnd_fills_from_sys.dram_io_near 3.996301634 seconds time elapsed Every load is 64 bytes (the minimum amount you can bring, a cache line), so we can multiply by 64 to see we pulled 4.5GB during this query from DRAM on CPU loads (this is without any prefetching). Let's now try to improve our algorithm to take advantage of the CPU caches. To do this, we'll use a method called radix partitioning. The idea is to split the merge into two distinct phases: Phase 1: In this phase, we're simply going to separate the keys into 4096 different partitions (simply a Vec of SlabVecs- a SlabVec is a data structure similar to a Vec that is above memory that is already paged in. We don't use Vecs for raw memory in Pivot because it creates a lot of variance; not something for this blog post!). The partition will be decided by hashing the key and taking it's top 12 bits (2**12=4096). fn consume ( & mut self , batch: RecordBatch , _sender: & mut dyn Sender < RecordBatch >, ) -> unary:: Result <()> { let keys = batch. column ( self .key_column). as_primitive ::< Int64Type >(); for &key in keys. values () { let hash = self .hasher. hash_one (key); // Since we want top 12 bits, we shift the hash (a u64) 52 bits to the right let partition = (hash >> 52 ) as usize; self .partitions[partition]. push (& mut self .allocator, (hash, key)); } Ok (()) } UserID hash(UserID) 7 0x 002 A91F3â¦ 42 0x 000 7C4E2â¦ 13 0x FFF 3B05Dâ¦ 7 0x 002 A91F3â¦ 5 0x 001 D6A88â¦ 42 0x 000 7C4E2â¦ 99 0x 002 E17B4â¦ 7 0x 002 A91F3â¦ â partition = hash >> 52 , the first 3 hex digits Partition 0 0x000000â¦ â 0x000FFFâ¦ 42 42 Partition 1 0x001000â¦ â 0x001FFFâ¦ 5 Partition 2 0x002000â¦ â 0x002FFFâ¦ 7 7 99 7   â¦ Partition 4095 0xFFF000â¦ â 0xFFFFFFâ¦ 13 Phase 2: When all data has come through, go partition by partition, each time creating a HashMap, aggregating the partition into it, and then outputting it. This phase is very similar to our original algorithm, but we're going to use the hash from phase 1. fn into_outputter ( self ) -> unary:: Result < Option < Self :: Outputter >> { let mut groups = Vec :: new (); for rows in & self .partitions { let mut table: HashTable <(u64, i64, u64)> = HashTable :: new (); // (hash, key, count) rows. for_each (|(hash, key)| { match table. entry (hash, |group| group. 1 == key, |group| group. 0 ) { Entry :: Occupied ( mut group) => group. get_mut (). 2 += 1 , Entry :: Vacant (slot) => { slot. insert ((hash, key, 1 )); } } }); groups. extend (table. into_iter (). map (|(_, key, count)| (key, count))); } Ok ( Some ( Outputter :: new (groups))) } Partitions, one at a time 0â1 done 2 in progress 3â4095 waiting Partition 2 HashTable Output 7 7 99 7 â UserID count 7 3 99 1 â (UserID, count) (7, 3) (99, 1) At first glance, this solution may seem rather odd. We're doing more operations here, not less! Every row, in both solutions, is hashed and sent into a HashMap. But in this solution, we're first pushing rows into seemingly meaningless vecs. The key here (no pun intended) is to understand why we've done this; it's to make the aggregating HashMaps smaller . By dividing our group by into 4096 pieces, we've made our working HashMaps much likelier to fit into our CPU caches. Every time we do a lookup on our HashMap, our CPU is more likely to find the relevant memory sitting in it's caches, which saves a big chunk of time. But why trust me? Let's run it! taskset -c 7 psql -h 127.0.0.1 -p 5440 -U pivot -c '\timing on' -c "SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT COUNT(*), UserID FROM hits GROUP BY UserID)" And... Boom! 3.3 seconds, and then on second run 2.7 seconds! We've definitely made an improvement. But to really drive this point home, let's run perf again: sudo perf stat -C 3 -M backend_bound_memory,retiring -- taskset -c 7 psql -h 127.0.0.1 -p 5440 -U pivot -c "SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT COUNT(*), UserID FROM hits GROUP BY UserID)" And our results: Performance counter stats for 'CPU(s) 3': 3790955223 ex_no_retire.load_not_complete # 23.5 % backend_bound_memory 20376118172 de_no_dispatch_per_slot.backend_stalls 5442424751 ex_no_retire.not_complete 10083617764 ls_not_halted_cyc 19350459182 ex_ret_ops # 32.2 % retiring 10023435553 ls_not_halted_cyc 3.575992317 seconds time elapsed Now we can see the picture has completely changed- 23.5% of the time is spent on waiting for memory (as opposed to 50% before), 32% for actually retiring operations. You may notice we're actually doing more work, not less- in this run, we did 19350459182 operations (the ex_ret_ops counter), whereas before the database did 11431618219 operations. This is worth it though, because as we said before- if we can translate cold DRAM accesses into CPU instructions, it's nearly always a good trade to make. In this case, we went down from 8364109137 CPU slots stalled because of memory to 3790955223. To complete the picture and really see we're pulling less memory from the DRAM, let's again check how many our memory loads come from DRAM: sudo perf stat -C 3 -e ls_dmnd_fills_from_sys.dram_io_near -- taskset -c 7 psql -h 127.0.0.1 -p 5440 -U pivot -c "SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT COUNT(*), UserID FROM hits GROUP BY UserID)" Performance counter stats for 'CPU(s) 3': 25688280 ls_dmnd_fills_from_sys.dram_io_near 3.009547012 seconds time elapsed Whoo! That means that on demand we pulled 1.5GB from DRAM, instead of 4.5GB in the naive version. That, of course, isn't the limit of how much we can utilize our CPU cache for GROUP BYs. And utilizing our CPU cache isn't the only way we can "hide" DRAM latency; another trick is prefetching memory to our cache before we need it, and yet another trick is creating algorithms that allow maximization of memory throughput- but that's not for this blog! We'll go into that in our next blog where we look at our /seemingly very weird/ implementation of JOIN probing. For now, without explaining too much, I'll leave you with Pivot's speed for this query on a single core: Time: 1848.353 ms (00:01.848) and the amount of RAM we bring: Performance counter stats for 'CPU(s) 3': 14917958 ls_dmnd_fills_from_sys.dram_io_near 2.182674864 seconds time elapsed Which comes out to 954 MB. Of course, Pivot knows to run in parallel on our 16 cores (where there are many other interesting cases), in which case it comes out to: Time: 171.773 ms nice :) Try out Pivot if you want to have super speeds above parquets (OSS fun!), see you next time. â All posts Â© 2026 Epsio Labs

title: TCP Use-After-Free: CVE-2026-98432 / CVSS 9.8
body_text: Linux's October 2026 TCP Use-After-Free: CVE-2026-98432 — Atlas Services About Meridian Audit Contact Client Portal About Meridian Audit Contact Services Systems Architecting the future — Turning abstract visions into functional, scalable reality. All Services Client Portal On this page, current section: On this page Overview Key facts Who is affected Distribution status How the vulnerability works The fix Which servers are exposed How to check your systems Check the kernel Check for multipath TCP listeners How to fix Update the kernel and reboot If you can't patch yet Timeline and exploitation status Updates to this post Get help Sources Back to the Meridian Home / Meridian / Security / Linux's October 2026 TCP Use-After-Free: CVE-2026-98432 Security Disclosure Fixed upstream · Oct 15, 2026 Linux kernel · IPv4 TCP handshake CVE-2026- 98432 Severity · Critical Remote use-after-free · CVSS 9.8 Release line Fixed in Supported until 7.3 7.3 — 7.2 7.2.10 — 6.18 6.18.56 — 6.12 6.12.113 — 5.10 – 6.6 5.10.272 – 6.6.159 — 4.4 – 5.4 distro fixes only — fixed no fix atlas · disclosure · Linux kernel Security · Security Disclosure Linux's October 2026 TCP Use-After-Free: CVE-2026-98432 CVE-2026-98432 is a CVSS 9.8 remote use-after-free in Linux's IPv4 TCP handshake, fixed upstream Oct 15. RHEL and AlmaLinux have fixes; Ubuntu doesn't yet. A Atlas Security Security Advisories · October 29, 2026 11:00 AM CDT · 18 min read · 3,845 words · Updated November 2, 2026, 12:00 PM CST Updated November 2, 2026 What changed AlmaLinux moved fixed kernels for AlmaLinux 8, 9, and 10 into production on November 2, a day after Red Hat shipped RHEL's. Ubuntu still has none. Turning off multipath TCP doesn't fix the bug. Anthropic's root exploit needed a multipath TCP listener, but the bug is in plain IPv4 TCP, and the Go Security Team says it's "possible that systems with no MPTCP listeners are vulnerable to similar attacks." What changed Trevor Fannin @ trvrio · Founder, Atlas Security alerts and CVE breakdowns, plus infrastructure and general tech. Follow on X (opens in a new tab) # Overview Linux's stable kernels shipped a fix on October 11 and 15, 2026 for CVE-2026-98432 , a use-after-free in the IPv4 TCP handshake that a remote, unauthenticated peer can reach. The kernel's own CVE Numbering Authority (CNA) scores it CVSS 3.1 9.8, Critical . The fixed releases are 5.10.272, 5.15.223, 6.1.190, 6.6.159, 6.12.113, 6.18.56, 7.2.10 , and 7.3 , and the bug goes back to Linux 4.4. The upstream fix is a four-line change, but most servers run a distribution's kernel. Red Hat, which now rates the bug Critical too, shipped fixed kernels for Red Hat Enterprise Linux (RHEL) 8, 9, and 10 on November 1, and AlmaLinux followed on November 2. As of 12:00 PM CST on November 2, Ubuntu's tracker still reads "Vulnerable" for its kernel on every release. CVE-2026-98432 · Linux kernel Critical · CVSS 9.8 Affected Linux from 4.4 on, below 5.10.272 / 5.15.223 / 6.1.190 / 6.6.159 / 6.12.113 / 6.18.56 / 7.2.10 . Distribution kernels follow their own versions: check the tracker. Fix Install your distribution's fixed kernel and reboot . Debian, RHEL, AlmaLinux, current SUSE Enterprise, Oracle UEK, and Amazon Linux kernels have one; Ubuntu's don't yet. Can't patch yet Drop TCP packets that carry IPv4 options ( Atlas's interim rule ), turn off multipath TCP if you don't use it, and patch hosts with multipath TCP listeners first. Why it's urgent: the bug sits in code every Linux server runs when it accepts an IPv4 TCP connection, before any application sees the connection. Anthropic, whose researcher reported it, says its Claude model wrote a working proof-of-concept exploit that runs commands as root on "Linux servers with a multipath TCP listener," with no credentials. Go programs open those listeners by default, per the Go Security Team. See the timeline . # Key facts Field Detail CVE CVE-2026-98432, "ipv4: free inet_opt and ireq_opt after an RCU grace period," issued by the Linux kernel CNA Severity Critical, CVSS 3.1 9.8 ( AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H ), the kernel CNA's score. Red Hat also rates it Critical, CVSS 3.1 9.8, raised from Important (8.1) on October 30. SUSE rates it important, Ubuntu rates it High, and Oracle and Amazon rate it Important with CVSS 3.1 8.1. Weakness Use-after-free of IPv4 option data during the TCP handshake (the record lists no CWE) Impact Per the CNA's scoring notes: kernel heap contents disclosed to the remote peer, kernel memory corruption, or a crash. Red Hat's bulletin: a remote, unauthenticated attacker "could exploit a race condition during TCP connection request processing to trigger remote code execution." Fixed in 7.2.10 and 6.18.56 (Oct 11) · 6.12.113, 6.6.159, 6.1.190, 5.15.223, and 5.10.272 (Oct 15) · 7.3 (Oct 18) No fix yet Ubuntu (every release), as of 12:00 PM CST, November 2. Red Hat fixed RHEL 8, 9, and 10 on November 1 but still lists OpenShift's RHEL CoreOS as affected. Upstream branches that reached end-of-life before 5.10 get no fix. Proof of concept Anthropic says Claude built a remote root exploit for servers with a multipath TCP listener. It hasn't published the exploit. CVE records Published on cve.org on October 15. NVD lists it as "Received," with no analysis of its own, as of 12:00 PM CST, November 2. Credit Reported by Xinyang Ge of Anthropic. Fixed by Eric Dumazet and reviewed by Kuniyuki Iwashima, per the fix commit. # Who is affected Any Linux kernel from 4.4 on that lacks the fix, whether it serves the network directly or hosts containers: a container runs on the host's kernel, so a new image doesn't change anything. IPv6 connections aren't affected by the main issue; the commit says "IPv6 is not affected by the first issue." Release line Status on Nov 2, 2026 Fixed in Released 7.3 Stable 7.3 (from 7.3-rc7) Oct 18, 2026 7.2 End of life (last release 7.2.15, Nov 1) 7.2.10 Oct 11, 2026 6.18 Longterm 6.18.56 Oct 11, 2026 6.12 Longterm 6.12.113 Oct 15, 2026 6.6 Longterm 6.6.159 Oct 15, 2026 6.1 Longterm 6.1.190 Oct 15, 2026 5.15 Longterm 5.15.223 Oct 15, 2026 5.10 Longterm 5.10.272 Oct 15, 2026 4.4 – 5.4 End-of-life upstream distro fixes only — # Distribution status Distribution kernels carry backported fixes under their own version numbers, so check the tracker, not the upstream number. As of 12:00 PM CST, November 2: Ubuntu: the tracker lists the linux package as "Vulnerable" on every release. On 26.10, 26.04, 24.04, and 22.04 it adds "work in progress" in 7.3.0-10.10 , 7.0.0-43.43 , 6.8.0-149.149 , and 5.15.0-203.213 ; 20.04, 18.04, and 16.04 show only "Vulnerable." Many cloud and hardware-enablement kernels are listed the same way, and no Ubuntu Security Notice has been published. Red Hat: rated Critical, CVSS 3.1 9.8, since October 30. Fixed kernels shipped on November 1 for RHEL 8.10 ( kernel-4.18.0-553.182.1.el8_10 , RHSA-2026:93414 , and its real-time kernel, RHSA-2026:93415 ), RHEL 9.8 ( kernel-5.14.0-687.64.1.el9_8 , RHSA-2026:93412 ), and RHEL 10.2 ( kernel-6.12.0-211.72.1.el10_2 , RHSA-2026:93413 ). The RHEL 9 and 10 updates include their real-time kernels. OpenShift Container Platform 4 and 5, through RHEL CoreOS, and RHEL for NVIDIA are still listed as affected, as is a separate RHEL 9 kernel-rt package; RHEL 6 and 7 aren't affected ( CVE page ). Its bulletin, RHSB-2026-016 , gives an nftables mitigation ( compared below ) and says any product that relies on the RHEL kernel, including RHEL CoreOS, "is also potentially impacted." AlmaLinux: fixed kernels for AlmaLinux 8, 9, and 10 reached its production repositories early on November 2: kernel-4.18.0-553.182.1.el8_10 , kernel-5.14.0-687.64.1.el9_8 , and kernel-6.12.0-211.72.1.el10_2 , the same versions as RHEL's ( announcement ). Its errata list them for AlmaLinux 8 (ALSA-2026:93414, and ALSA-2026:93415 for the real-time kernel) but not yet for 9 or 10. The kernels it put in its testing repository on October 30 also carry the fix. Debian: fixed in 12 "bookworm" ( 6.1.190-1 , DLA-4841-1, and linux-6.12 6.12.113-1~deb12u1 , DLA-4850-1), 13 "trixie" ( 6.12.113-1 , DSA-6568-1), and unstable ( tracker ). SUSE: rated important. SUSE Linux Enterprise Server 16.0 ( kernel-default 6.12.0-160000.40.1 ) and the 15 SP4, SP5, and SP6 LTSS kernels are fixed; 15 SP7 is in progress. openSUSE Leap 16.0 is fixed, and Leap 15.6 is listed as affected ( CVE page ). Oracle Linux: rated Important, CVSS 3.1 8.1. Unbreakable Enterprise Kernel (UEK) errata for Oracle Linux 7, 8, 9, and 10 came out October 16: ELSA-2026-500397, ELSA-2026-500398, and ELSA-2026-500399 ( CVE page ). On November 2, Oracle added its Red Hat Compatible Kernel for Oracle Linux 10 ( kernel-6.12.0-211.72.1.el10_2 , ELSA-2026-93413) and Oracle Linux 8 ( kernel-4.18.0-553.182.1.el8_10 , ELSA-2026-93414); the page lists none yet for Oracle Linux 9. Amazon Linux: rated Important, CVSS 3.1 8.1, and every kernel is fixed. On Amazon Linux 2023, the default kernel (ALAS2023-2026-3365, October 30), kernel6.12 (ALAS2023-2026-3335, October 29), and kernel6.18 (ALAS2023-2026-3251, October 24). On Amazon Linux 2, the core kernel (ALAS2-2026-4065) and the 5.4, 5.10, and 5.15 Extras kernels (ALAS2KERNEL-5.4-2026-135, ALAS2KERNEL-5.10-2026-137, and ALAS2KERNEL-5.15-2026-120), all October 30 ( CVE page ). AWS's bulletin adds that Amazon Linux 2023 instances locked to a release version need release 2023.12.20261102 or later, and that EKS-optimized Amazon Linux 2023 AMIs from release v20261031 and ECS-optimized AMIs from release 20261031 carry the fix. # How the vulnerability works When a Linux server accepts a TCP connection, the kernel tracks the half-open handshake in a lightweight "request socket," then creates a full socket once the handshake completes. If the connecting peer's IPv4 header carried options, the kernel keeps them to echo in its replies. The bug: the kernel handed those saved options from the request socket to the new connection without copying them, then freed them immediately when the connection went away, while another CPU could still be reading them to build a handshake reply. Reading freed kernel memory is a use-after-free. The peer needs no login, and it all happens inside the kernel's handshake handling, before any application code runs. The CNA's scoring notes say the stale data can leak kernel heap memory back to the peer, steer kernel writes out of bounds, or crash the machine. Anthropic says a lost race "only fails the handshake without crashing the whole system, so a determined attacker can retry indefinitely until they succeed." # The fix Eric Dumazet's commit, "ipv4: free inet_opt and ireq_opt after an RCU grace period," changes two plain kfree() calls to kfree_rcu() , which waits until every reader has finished with the memory before freeing it. Other code paths that replace these options already did that. The commit also fixes the same problem in request-socket migration ( net.ipv4.tcp_migrate_req=1 , or a BPF_SK_REUSEPORT_SELECT_OR_MIGRATE program), and says a related IPv6 case "will be addressed in a separate patch." ipv4: free inet_opt and ireq_opt after an RCU grace period torvalds/linux · e3f33b0 · Oct 1, 2026 net/ipv4/af_inet.c + 1 − 1 1 lines added, 1 removed net/ipv4/tcp_ipv4.c + 1 − 1 1 lines added, 1 removed 2 files changed + 2 − 2 2 lines added, 2 removed # Which servers are exposed Every Linux host that accepts IPv4 TCP connections on an affected kernel: web servers, SSH, databases, load balancers, and Kubernetes nodes. The CNA's notes say the vulnerable path runs "during the TCP handshake, before application authentication." Hosts with a multipath TCP (MPTCP) listener first. That's the setup Anthropic's working exploit needs: "Linux servers with a multipath TCP listener." Anthropic hasn't said why that listener matters, and the CVE record doesn't mention MPTCP. A server has one only if an application opens an MPTCP socket, and Go programs do by default: the Go Security Team says "as of Go 1.24, Go programs enable MPTCP by default for listen sockets on Linux." The default follows the go line in the program's go.mod , and applies only where the kernel allows MPTCP ( net.mptcp.enabled = 1 , as on the Debian 12 kernel we checked; AlmaLinux says it ships MPTCP off). The Go team adds that "the underlying bug is not specific to MPTCP. It is possible that systems with no MPTCP listeners are vulnerable to similar attacks." The check is below . Hosts behind a pass-through load balancer. AWS's bulletin says its Network Load Balancer TCP listeners "pass client packets, including IP options, to targets," and tells customers to patch the Linux hosts behind them, and behind Global Accelerator, PrivateLink endpoint services, and VPC Lattice TCP listeners. Behind Application Load Balancer, CloudFront, or API Gateway, it says, customers "do not receive TCP connections from untrusted sources directly when following best practices." Red Hat now rates it as the CNA does. It raised the bug from Important (8.1) to Critical (9.8) on October 30, citing "the lack of network prerequisites and the potential for severe system instability." Its bulletin says "Systems accepting inbound TCP connections are most directly exposed." # How to check your systems # Check the kernel Shell Copy 1 uname - r # the running kernel 2 uname - v # Debian: the package version running 3 dpkg - l 'linux-image*' | grep ^ ii # Debian/Ubuntu: installed kernel packages 4 rpm - q kernel # RHEL and derivatives: installed kernels 5 needs-restarting - r # RHEL (dnf-utils): is a reboot needed? Compare the result with your distribution's status above , not with the upstream version. If the installed kernel is newer than the running one, the fix isn't active until you reboot. Run these on container hosts and Kubernetes nodes, not inside containers: a container reports the host's kernel. We ran them on a Debian 12 host and in a Rocky Linux 9 container. # Check for multipath TCP listeners Shell Copy 1 ss - Mlnp # MPTCP listening sockets and the processes that own them 2 sysctl net . mptcp . enabled # 1 means applications may open MPTCP sockets ss -M lists only MPTCP sockets, so an empty result means no MPTCP listener. net.mptcp.enabled = 1 alone doesn't create one: an application has to open an MPTCP socket. We tested both with iproute2 6.1 in a Debian 12 container, where ss -Mlnp listed a test MPTCP listener and skipped a plain TCP one beside it. On October 31 it also listed a Go HTTP server whose go.mod says go 1.24 , and skipped the same server built with go 1.23 . # How to fix # Update the kernel and reboot Install your distribution's fixed kernel as soon as it ships, then reboot: a kernel update doesn't take effect until the machine boots into it. Reboot container hosts and Kubernetes nodes too. Appliances and cloud images that bundle a kernel need their vendor's update. On Debian, RHEL and AlmaLinux 8, 9, and 10, SUSE Linux Enterprise Server 16.0 and the 15 LTSS releases, openSUSE Leap 16.0, Oracle Linux's UEK kernels, and Amazon Linux 2 and 2023, the fix is out. On Ubuntu and OpenShift's RHEL CoreOS, it isn't out yet, as of 12:00 PM CST, November 2. Watch the trackers linked above . Running a self-built kernel? Move to the fixed stable release for its line. # If you can't patch yet Red Hat's bulletin and AlmaLinux now publish nftables rules that drop incoming IPv4 TCP packets carrying IP options. Red Hat says its rule "reduces exposure to this vulnerability but cannot fully prevent it." The following is Atlas's interim recommendation, the same rule as AlmaLinux's, based on the CNA's scoring notes, which say the attacking peer supplies IPv4 Record Route or Timestamp options in its SYN. TCP traffic almost never carries IPv4 options legitimately, so dropping TCP packets that have them should cost nothing: Shell Copy 1 nft add table ip cve_2026_98432 2 nft add chain ip cve_2026_98432 pre '{ type filter hook prerouting priority -300; }' 3 nft add rule ip cve_2026_98432 pre meta l4proto tcp ip hdrlength gt 5 counter drop ip hdrlength gt 5 matches any IPv4 header longer than the 20-byte minimum, which only options produce. The rule runs before connection tracking and doesn't touch IPv6 or non-TCP traffic. We tested it in a Debian 12 container: it dropped a SYN carrying a Record Route option, and ordinary TCP connections still worked. We haven't tested it against an exploit, and it doesn't fix the kernel. It lasts until reboot, which is fine if the reboot is into a fixed kernel; remove it with nft delete table ip cve_2026_98432 . If your edge firewall can drop IPv4 packets with options, doing it there protects every host behind it. If you manage the firewall with iptables, this rule does the same job from the raw table, which also runs before connection tracking: Shell Copy 1 iptables - t raw - I PREROUTING - p tcp - m u32 - - u32 "0>>24&0xF=6:15" - j DROP The u32 match reads the IPv4 header-length field, and a value of 6 to 15 means the header carries options. We tested it with iptables 1.8.9, on both its nf_tables and legacy backends, in a Debian 12 container: it dropped a Record Route SYN sent to the host and one routed through it, and ordinary TCP connections still worked. Remove it by running the same command with -D in place of -I ; like the nft rule, it lasts until reboot. It needs the kernel's xt_u32 module, which the Debian 12, Ubuntu 22.04 and 24.04, and RHEL 8 kernels include. RHEL 9 and 10 kernels, and their rebuilds, leave it out, so use the nft rule there. Red Hat's rule hooks input ; ours hooks prerouting , so it also drops packets the host routes on to containers. On October 31 we tested it against two pairs of network namespaces. It dropped a Record Route SYN routed between one pair, and never saw one bridged between the other, as AlmaLinux warns: "Traffic between containers on the same host may bypass it." AlmaLinux also says not to use it on networks that rely on CIPSO security labels, which travel in IPv4 options. Turn off multipath TCP if you don't use it. That removes the setup Anthropic's exploit needs, though not the bug. AlmaLinux's steps: Shell Copy 1 echo 'net.mptcp.enabled = 0' | sudo tee / etc / sysctl . d / 9 0 - disable-mptcp . conf 2 sudo sysctl - w net . mptcp . enabled = 0 3 sudo ss - Mlnp # listeners opened earlier stay MPTCP: restart their services New MPTCP sockets then fail, and Go programs fall back to plain TCP when they start. The setting is per network namespace, and each new one starts with MPTCP on, so a container keeps it unless you set it there too (Docker: --sysctl net.mptcp.enabled=0 ). We tested the steps and the Docker flag on October 31. For a single Go program, GODEBUG=multipathtcp=0 in its environment turns the default off, but the Go Security Team calls disabling MPTCP program by program "a fragile mitigation." Until you can patch, keep MPTCP listeners off the internet, and put the hosts that have one at the top of the patch list. # Timeline and exploitation status All times are US Central: CDT (UTC−5) through October 31, CST (UTC−6) from November 1. When What Oct 1 · 5:12 PM Eric Dumazet posts the fix, crediting Xinyang Ge of Anthropic as reporter Oct 5 The fix is merged into the kernel's networking tree Oct 11 Linux 7.2.10 and 6.18.56 ship the fix; 7.3-rc7 follows that night Oct 15 · 4:56–7:16 AM Linux 6.12.113, 6.6.159, 6.1.190, 5.15.223, and 5.10.272 ship the fix; the CVE record is published at 7:08 AM Oct 16 Oracle publishes UEK errata with the fix for Oracle Linux 7 through 10 Oct 18 Linux 7.3 is released with the fix Oct 24 Amazon Linux 2023's kernel6.18 package is fixed Oct 27 Anthropic's Frontier Red Team describes a remote root exploit for the bug, built by Claude in its lab Oct 29 · 6:34 PM The Go Security Team says Go programs have opened MPTCP listeners by default since Go 1.24 Oct 29 Ubuntu still lists its kernels as vulnerable; Amazon Linux 2023's kernel6.12 package is fixed; GitHub repositories referencing the CVE appear, one created at 7:22 PM describing a race trigger Oct 30 AlmaLinux puts fixed kernels in its testing repository; Red Hat raises its rating to Critical and publishes bulletin RHSB-2026-016 with a mitigation; Amazon Linux fixes its remaining kernels Oct 31 36 GitHub repositories reference the CVE, at least six describing a race trigger or a proof of concept Nov 1 · 2:52–4:16 PM Red Hat ships fixed kernels for RHEL 8, 9, and 10 Nov 1 Linux 7.2 reaches end of life with 7.2.15; 41 GitHub repositories reference the CVE, at least seven describing a race trigger or a proof of concept Nov 2 AlmaLinux moves fixed kernels for 8, 9, and 10 to its production repositories; Oracle fixes its Red Hat Compatible Kernel for Oracle Linux 8 and 10; 57 GitHub repositories reference the CVE, at least nine describing a race trigger or a proof of concept Exploitation status. Anthropic says Claude wrote the exploit "after initial prompting," that it runs "arbitrary commands as root, without any credentials or user interaction" on servers with a multipath TCP listener, and that in its proof of concept "it takes 48 minutes to leak a kernel pointer and another five minutes to reach the shell command execution." Anthropic hasn't published the exploit. Its disclosure policy gives developers 90 days to patch and a further 45 days before Anthropic discusses details beyond a public advisory. Red Hat's bulletin now says the bug could be exploited "to trigger remote code execution." By 12:00 PM CST on November 2, 57 GitHub repositories referenced the CVE. Most describe themselves as audit or mitigation tooling, among them Ansible roles, an XDP program, and a livepatch for AlmaLinux and Rocky Linux. At least nine say they include a race trigger or a proof of concept for the use-after-free; the first was created at 7:22 PM CDT on October 29, and the latest at 2:07 AM CST on November 2. That one calls itself a "lab root-shell kit" that needs a kernel modified to help the exploit, "not a stock remote exploit." The CVE isn't in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog as of 12:00 PM CST. We haven't tested any public proof of concept, and we aren't linking them. # Updates to this post We'll revise this post and mark it updated when any of these change: fixed kernels from Ubuntu or a fixed RHEL CoreOS for OpenShift; NVD's analysis; a KEV listing or any report of exploitation; the separate IPv6 fix. November 2, 12:00 PM CST: AlmaLinux moved fixed kernels for AlmaLinux 8, 9, and 10 from testing to its production repositories, the same versions as RHEL's, and Oracle fixed its Red Hat Compatible Kernel for Oracle Linux 8 and 10. Added AWS's bulletin: which of its load balancers pass IP options on to the hosts behind them, the Amazon Linux 2023 release that locked instances need, and its fixed EKS and ECS AMIs. 57 GitHub repositories now reference the CVE, at least nine describing a race trigger or a proof of concept. Ubuntu, Red Hat, Debian, SUSE, Amazon Linux's packages, NVD's status, and KEV are unchanged, and Linux 7.4-rc1, released November 1, doesn't include the IPv6 follow-up. November 1, 6:15 PM CST: Red Hat shipped fixed kernels for RHEL 8, 9, and 10, including the real-time kernels, between 2:52 and 4:16 PM, so RHEL moved out of the "no fix yet" row; OpenShift's RHEL CoreOS and RHEL for NVIDIA are still listed as affected. Linux 7.2 reached end of life with 7.2.15, and 7.3 is now a stable line. 41 GitHub repositories now reference the CVE, at least seven describing a race trigger or a proof of concept. Ubuntu, AlmaLinux, Debian, SUSE, Oracle, Amazon, NVD's status, and KEV are unchanged, and no IPv6 follow-up has landed in mainline or the stable kernels. October 31, 5:15 PM CDT: Red Hat raised its rating from Important (8.1) to Critical (9.8) on October 30 and published a mitigation in bulletin RHSB-2026-016, so we replaced its earlier rating and its "no mitigation" statement. Added the Go Security Team's notice that Go programs open MPTCP listeners by default, AlmaLinux's fixed kernels in testing, Amazon Linux's fixes for its remaining kernels, openSUSE Leap 16.0's fix, steps to turn off MPTCP, an iptables version of the interim rule, and the interim rule's limits with bridged container traffic and CIPSO. 36 GitHub repositories now reference the CVE. Ubuntu, Debian, Oracle, NVD's status, and KEV are unchanged, and the stable kernels released October 30 don't include the IPv6 follow-up. October 29, 8:00 PM CDT: Added Oracle Linux, fixed in its UEK kernels since October 16, and Amazon Linux, fixed in Amazon Linux 2023's 6.12 and 6.18 kernels and pending elsewhere. Eight GitHub repositories now reference the CVE, one describing a race trigger. Ubuntu, Red Hat, Debian, SUSE, NVD, and KEV are unchanged since 11:00 AM, and nothing was corrected. # Get help The bug is reachable through any listening TCP port, so it helps to know which ones the internet can see. Our free security audit checks the domains and public IPs you verify for exposed services, publicly visible software versions with known CVEs, TLS, email security, DNS, and HTTP headers. title: The AI cost of JavaScript frameworks
body_text: The AI cost of JavaScript frameworks | Read the Tea Leaves Skip to content Read the Tea Leaves Software and other dark arts, by Nolan Lawson Search this blog Search home apps code talks about Previous post: « Do web components have a future if nobody is writing them? 28 Oct The AI cost of JavaScript frameworks Posted October 28, 2026 by Nolan Lawson in Web , AI . One of my pet peeves with the web development community is that so many of the decisions we make are vibes-based. Frameworks are “blazing fast,” tools will “supercharge” your development, the right abstraction will benefit both you and your users ( DX and UX all in one!). All of this breathless boasting is usually offered with zero evidence. Alex Russell has called this “frontend’s lost decade” , Baldur Bjarnason has called programming a pop culture , and I’ve tried to counter this trend in my blog with facts and benchmarks (at my best, anyway). For a long time it seemed like our community’s allergy to evidence was driven by the desire for greater DX . In other words, devs just liked the way it felt to type JSX in React, and the arguments promoting React or related tools (“the virtual DOM is fast!”) were largely post-hoc rationalizations to justify those initial gut feelings. ( Jonathan Haidt would likely agree with this assessment.) But in the agentic era, when developers are no longer typing code by hand and are thus less constrained by DX, I still see vibes ruling the day (and not just in the sense of “vibe-coding”). Frontends are rewritten because some framework or another is “better for agents.” (Did anyone think to ask the agents?) The resulting code is “faster,” the agents make “fewer mistakes,” etc. Once again, these claims are often made without evidence. Whenever I read one of these accounts, I think to myself, “Where are the benchmarks?” Well I got curious, so I wrote a benchmark. The structure of this benchmark is pretty straightforward: Design a small but non-trivial Pokémon app using the PokéAPI (those who have followed my work will be unsurprised) Instruct agents to build the app with a particular JavaScript framework/meta-framework (e.g. Next.js, Nuxt, SvelteKit, etc.) Test the output against a spec conformance suite (to avoid agent cheating) Evaluate the results in terms of development time, tokens spent, lines of code, and performance and accessibility scores in Lighthouse The app is fairly simple: you’ve got a list of Pokémon with their types, moves, and data from various games. You can search, filter, etc.: I should start off with some caveats: this is not a perfect experiment. This app represents only one holotype – it’s a relatively content-based site with little interactivity, closer to a Wikipedia than a Figma, GMail, etc. That said, I had to choose some app to build, and this one is at least easy to understand at a high level, and relatively straightforward to spec out and test. To try to even the playing field, I had each framework/meta-framework use the official MCP or skills for that tool. I wanted to avoid accusations of “this framework is not well-represented in the training data, that’s why we built our MCP, we expect people to use it,” etc. I also didn’t over-specify the exact architecture to use (e.g. SSR vs CSR ), nor did I specify that the app should be as performant as possible. I simply gave the spec to Opus 5.5 with high effort and told it to use the latest version of the given framework. Each agent ran in a sandbox and without any knowledge that it would be tested in Lighthouse on performance and accessibility, although it was given the conformance test suite. Note I also didn’t mandate any CSS methodology, except to avoid using Tailwind, Bootstrap, or any other component framework, and to design based on a set of spec tokens to enforce some visual consistency. I didn’t want to make this test all about CSS, but instead about JS frameworks, CSR vs SSR, SPAs vs MPAs , etc. The resulting app is tested against a conformance suite based on the accessibility tree rather than the raw DOM to avoid mandating any particular HTML structure – one framework uses web components which rely on shadow DOM, so this was required. One thing I learned from this experiment is that everything I’m measuring is very stochastic. LLMs are random-word generators, so sometimes you get a low dice-roll and an agent goes off on some weird tangent wasting a bunch of tokens, through no fault of the framework or its tools. Lighthouse itself can give inconsistent results as well: Largest Contentful Paint (LCP) may decide that one image is the “largest” element, then pick another one on the next run. It’s hard to have a perfectly fair experiment, but running multiple iterations did help, and I’ve tried to be honest about the variance. With all that throat-clearing out of the way, let’s get to the results. Results I’m going to break this down by multiple dimensions: cost to build, quality, and maintainability. For each framework/meta-framework, I took the median of 5 runs: in other words, I built the same app 5 times in the same framework. (Yes, this is the kind of zany thing you can do with coding agents these days.) The exception was Angular, which failed to create a measurable app twice, so I took 3 iterations instead for some metrics. (This is explained below.) Cost Cost per run, in US dollars Framework Cost ($) Hono+htmx $2.67 (2.23–3.19) −0.44 +0.52 Astro $2.76 (2.16–3.63) −0.60 +0.87 Nuxt $2.82 (2.39–4.25) −0.43 +1.43 Vanilla $2.98 (2.24–3.37) −0.74 +0.39 Next.js $3.14 (2.58–4.13) −0.56 +0.99 Qwik $3.27 (2.35–3.80) −0.92 +0.53 TanStack Start $3.54 (3.11–3.96) −0.43 +0.42 SolidStart $3.79 (2.84–4.81) −0.95 +1.02 React Router $3.81 (2.82–3.97) −0.99 +0.16 SvelteKit $4.28 (3.59–4.65) −0.69 +0.37 Gracile+Lit $4.65 (3.92–5.07) −0.73 +0.42 Angular $4.97 (3.19–6.82) −1.78 +1.85 0 2 4 6 8 Median of 5 runs. Sort Original order Framework, A–Z Cost ($), low to high Cost ($), high to low Show as table Note that this quotes the API prices directly from Claude Code and doesn’t actually represent how much money I spent. I’m on a Max plan, so this was just part of my overall $100/month. Note also the variance: React Router’s median is roughly $1 worse than that of Hono+htmx, but the cheapest version of React Router ($2.82) is still cheaper than the most expensive version of Hono+htmx ($3.19). However some reliable patterns do emerge. Most clearly, SvelteKit, Gracile+Lit, and Angular are more expensive to build than the other frameworks. For SvelteKit, this may be due to the fact that the agents read the SvelteKit v3 migration guide in every run, likely because it’s too new to be in Opus 5.5’s training data. Similarly for Gracile, the agents didn’t know the framework very well and either cloned the Gracile repo or read its compiled source from node_modules . For Angular it seems to be a function of the total code size (see below). I should also mention that not every agent made use of an MCP/skill/Claude Code plugin, nor did every framework have one: Click to see AI tool usage Framework Installed Used by the agents? Angular Angular MCP and Angular agent skills MCP in 3/5 runs, skill tool in 4/5 runs, skill files in 2/5 Astro Astro MCP server MCP in 2/5 runs Gracile+Lit N/A N/A Hono+htmx Hono skills Skill tool in 5/5 runs Next.js next-devtools-mcp and next-dev-loop skill Skill files in 1/5 runs, AGENTS.md in 2/5 runs Nuxt Nuxt MCP N/A Qwik N/A N/A React Router React Router skill Skill tool in 5/5 runs, skill files in 5/5 runs SolidStart N/A N/A SvelteKit Svelte Claude Code plugin MCP in 5/5 runs TanStack Start N/A Skill files in 2/5 runs Vanilla N/A N/A For example, TanStack Start’s agent only discovered its skill files in 2/5 runs (they’re shipped in the node_modules of the project). For Nuxt, the MCP was never used by the agents. For Next.js, agents only read the skill file in 1/5 runs and the AGENTS.md in 2/5 runs. This is a wide range of results, which points back to the stochastic nature of LLMs. I still consider this a valid experiment, though, because I doubt many vibe-coders are shouting at their agents in all-caps to use the MCP (and plenty are probably skipping it entirely). Also, if you’re wondering how I came up with Hono+htmx: essentially, I wanted htmx represented somehow, and Hono seemed like a fine pairing (i.e. as a JavaScript alternative to Rails/Django/etc.). As for Gracile+Lit, I wanted web components represented via their standard-bearer framework (Lit), and was only aware of Gracile as a meta-framework. If there are better candidates, then those would be great for a follow-up experiment. For “Vanilla,” note that the agent was told to use “vanilla JavaScript or TypeScript with Vite, without a UI framework.” Surprisingly, this underperforms several frameworks, which seems to demonstrate that having some framework can be better than nothing (or better than raw Vite, anyway). Vite was chosen because it undergirds many frameworks and represents fairly standard and agnostic JavaScript infrastructure. The total time and tokens track pretty closely with the cost: Time per run Framework Time (minutes) Astro 8.2 min (6.2–9.7) −2.0 +1.5 Hono+htmx 8.6 min (5.9–9.6) −2.7 +1.0 Nuxt 9.0 min (8.0–17.6) −1.0 +8.6 Vanilla 10.1 min (6.9–18.6) −3.2 +8.5 TanStack Start 10.3 min (8.3–13.9) −2.0 +3.6 Qwik 10.7 min (7.1–12.9) −3.6 +2.2 SvelteKit 10.8 min (8.6–13.8) −2.2 +3.0 Next.js 10.9 min (8.3–11.9) −2.6 +1.0 SolidStart 11.2 min (8.2–15.9) −3.0 +4.7 Gracile+Lit 12.1 min (10.8–12.9) −1.3 +0.8 React Router 12.5 min (8.4–13.6) −4.1 +1.1 Angular 17.2 min (9.8–23.7) −7.4 +6.5 0 5 10 15 20 25 Wall-clock minutes from the agent’s perspective. Median of 5 runs. Sort Original order Framework, A–Z Time (minutes), low to high Time (minutes), high to low Show as table Tokens per run, in millions Framework Tokens (M) Nuxt 3.85 M (3.16–8.18) −0.69 +4.33 Astro 4.13 M (3.03–7.57) −1.10 +3.44 Hono+htmx 4.26 M (3.40–5.61) −0.86 +1.35 Next.js 4.99 M (3.54–8.82) −1.45 +3.83 Vanilla 5.00 M (3.44–6.32) −1.56 +1.32 Qwik 5.64 M (3.41–7.03) −2.23 +1.39 TanStack Start 7.07 M (5.85–7.99) −1.22 +0.92 SolidStart 7.13 M (5.02–10.07) −2.11 +2.94 React Router 7.58 M (4.55–8.18) −3.03 +0.60 SvelteKit 8.53 M (6.79–9.29) −1.74 +0.76 Gracile+Lit 9.04 M (7.36–11.10) −1.68 +2.06 Angular 9.76 M (4.92–14.94) −4.84 +5.18 0 5 10 15 Cache reads, uncached input and output. Median of 5 runs. Sort Original order Framework, A–Z Tokens (M), low to high Tokens (M), high to low Show as table The tokens, by the way, were reported by Claude Code. The duration is just the total wall-clock time. Quality Of course, because I think that outcomes matter, I also tested the agents with Lighthouse. As software developers, I think it’s important that we not only build things cheaply but also performantly and accessibly. I should first note two caveats about my benchmark: The Pokémon app is small and doesn’t represent a large, complex real-world application. Lighthouse and the Core Web Vitals in general are biased against SPAs, so the MPA frameworks are almost guaranteed to win on metrics like Total Blocking Time (TBT), JavaScript bytes, etc. I considered adding some in-app performance metrics but backed off because it added complexity and variability to the benchmark, and these would be metrics I invented as opposed to industry standards. For simplicity’s sake, I’m only reporting the scores for the home page. There are other pages, but they all score fairly similarly or they have wild swings in metrics like LCP, so it just complicates things to include them. In short: the Lighthouse scores for Performance, Accessibility, and CLS (Cumulative Layout Shift) are nearly saturated and don’t vary much by framework: Framework CLS Performance Accessibility Angular 0.000 98 100 Astro 0.000 100 100 Gracile+Lit 0.000 100 100 Hono+htmx 0.000 100 100 Next.js 0.000 99 100 Nuxt 0.000 100 100 Qwik 0.000 100 100 React Router 0.000 100 100 SolidStart 0.000 100 100 SvelteKit 0.000 100 100 TanStack Start 0.000 99 100 Vanilla 0.111 97 100 So to get some more interesting numbers, we need to look at other metrics. The most reliable one is the JavaScript bytes sent, which largely tracks the client-side framework size: JavaScript bytes transferred Framework JS (KiB) Astro 0 KiB (0–1) −0 +1 Vanilla 7 KiB (6–7) −1 +0 Gracile+Lit 8 KiB (1–13) −7 +5 Hono+htmx 18 KiB (18–18) −0 +0 SvelteKit 36 KiB (35–36) −1 +0 SolidStart 40 KiB (38–40) −2 +0 Qwik 40 KiB (40–41) −0 +1 Nuxt 84 KiB (83–85) −1 +1 Angular 93 KiB (81–102) −12 +9 React Router 115 KiB (115–119) −0 +4 TanStack Start 118 KiB (112–119) −6 +1 Next.js 142 KiB (136–143) −6 +1 0 50 100 150 As reported by Lighthouse. Median of 5 apps (3 for Angular). Sort Original order Framework, A–Z JS (KiB), low to high JS (KiB), high to low Show as table The Total Blocking Time (TBT) is interesting in that it’s not purely a function of the JavaScript bytes; some of the apps spend more time on the main thread than others. That said, the numbers are all quite small: Total Blocking Time (TBT) Framework TBT (ms) Astro 0 ms (0–0) −0 +0 Gracile+Lit 0 ms (0–0) −0 +0 Hono+htmx 0 ms (0–0) −0 +0 SvelteKit 0 ms (0–1) −0 +1 Vanilla 0 ms (0–0) −0 +0 TanStack Start 1 ms (0–36) −1 +35 Qwik 3 ms (0–30) −3 +27 SolidStart 11 ms (0–12) −11 +1 React Router 17 ms (0–52) −17 +35 Nuxt 40 ms (14–54) −26 +14 Next.js 71 ms (66–121) −5 +50 Angular 103 ms (93–123) −10 +20 0 25 50 75 100 125 As reported by Lighthouse, simulated mobile throttling. Median of 5 Lighthouse runs per app, then median of 5 apps after that (3 for Angular). Sort Original order Framework, A–Z TBT (ms), low to high TBT (ms), high to low Show as table Largest Contentful Paint (LCP) is highly variable due to the aforementioned issues with the metric itself. As expected, though, it does broadly punish SPAs and reward MPAs: Largest Contentful Paint (LCP) Framework LCP (ms) Astro 810 ms (792–1662) −18 +852 Gracile+Lit 956 ms (796–980) −160 +24 Hono+htmx 978 ms (977–1662) −1 +684 Qwik 979 ms (954–1278) −25 +299 SvelteKit 1130 ms (1129–1131) −1 +1 SolidStart 1204 ms (1203–1278) −1 +74 Vanilla 1667 ms (764–1676) −903 +9 Nuxt 1727 ms (1427–1844) −300 +117 React Router 1729 ms (1729–1770) −0 +41 Angular 1954 ms (1351–1955) −603 +1 TanStack Start 2028 ms (1805–2104) −223 +76 Next.js 2090 ms (1028–2187) −1062 +97 0 500 1000 1500 2000 2500 As reported by Lighthouse, simulated mobile throttling. Median of 5 Lighthouse runs per app, then median of 5 apps after that (3 for Angular). Sort Original order Framework, A–Z LCP (ms), low to high LCP (ms), high to low Show as table Test environment: 2025 Framework 13 Laptop on Ubuntu 24.04, 4x CPU throttling, and “Slow 4G” network throttling. I only ran Lighthouse’s mobile tests, not its desktop tests. Note that the wild variance in the Next.js numbers can be explained by the fact that one app avoided lazy-loading images and the other four didn’t . Astro and Vanilla have similar swings that appear to be caused by prioritization or LCP quirks. In general though, it’s unsurprising that the metric tends to reward MPAs that paint quickly with HTML rather than SPAs that paint after client-side JavaScript runs (along with possibly multiple throttled round-trips to grab the Pokémon data). Ignoring variance, LCP here is mostly a function of JavaScript bundle size. (Qwik is a notable exception here: technically it’s an SPA that uses client-side routing, but it scores among the MPA frameworks.) Note though that some of the frameworks varied in whether they focused more on the client or the server, or even whether they used a client-side framework. For example, the Gracile agent didn’t even use Lit in two runs . For “Vanilla,” the agent had full latitude (aside from being told to use Vite), but still chose to build an SPA all 5 times. SSR vs CSR is also partly where the trouble with Angular came from: in 2 runs, the agent built an SSR app that rejected non-localhost (even though the instructions explicitly said that the app would be behind a reverse proxy). I considered this a valid failure to adhere to the spec and decided not to re-run the 2 failed iterations. (This only affects the code size and performance measurements; I have reported all 5 Angular iterations for the “cost” section.) Maintainability There are lots of ways to measure maintainability (including fancy things like cyclomatic complexity), but I decided to keep it simple and report something tried-and-true: total lines of code. Lines of code Framework Lines of code Hono+htmx 1370 (1264–1489) −106 +119 Nuxt 1415 (1382–1458) −33 +43 Astro 1461 (1379–1503) −82 +42 Vanilla 1492 (1437–1742) −55 +250 Next.js 1539 (1452–1627) −87 +88 React Router 1564 (1421–1621) −143 +57 SvelteKit 1611 (1503–1816) −108 +205 SolidStart 1630 (1528–1894) −102 +264 TanStack Start 1697 (1506–1771) −191 +74 Gracile+Lit 1717 (1412–1748) −305 +31 Qwik 1744 (1646–1827) −98 +83 Angular 2009 (2003–2051) −6 +42 0 500 1000 1500 2000 2500 Number of non-blank source file lines. Median of 5 apps (3 for Angular). Sort Original order Framework, A–Z Lines of code, low to high Lines of code, high to low Show as table To me this is one of the more interesting charts. In a sense, the whole point of a framework is to reduce the amount of code you need to maintain. In Rich Harris’s memorable words: “Frameworks are not tools for organizing your code; they are tools for organizing your mind.” – Rich Harris, “Rethinking reactivity” In the agentic era, this hits even harder because the code size ultimately impacts the number of tokens, including in future edits, meaning it affects the literal cost to maintain a codebase over time. This doesn’t mean that succinctness is the only value that matters, but it’s certainly interesting to see that Hono+htmx can do roughly the same thing as Angular with ~70% of the code (and faster, to boot). Conclusion There are many ways you could improve this benchmark. For example, you could mandate that the agent use Service Workers for offline caching, or optimize the Pokémon image files, or use lazy-loading, fetchpriority , the Speculation Rules API, etc. Even though I know a lot of these performance hacks, I deliberately didn’t steer the agents toward any of them, because it’s not what a typical vibe-coder would do. On the other hand, this entire benchmark could be cheated by just pre-generating all the HTML files as static assets (there are only so many Pokémon). I specifically forebade that in the instructions and made it an explicit check in the test harness, because I felt that it wasn’t in the spirit of the benchmark. (My aim is to simulate a large volume of possibly-dynamic data, which is more challenging than a purely static site.) You could also improve the way I ran the benchmark by running more iterations, using different coding agents, trying different effort levels, using different frameworks or different versions of the frameworks, trying with and without MCPs/skills, testing in more browsers than just Chromium, building different types of apps, etc. I didn’t do these things mostly in the interest of time. However, if anybody wants to run the benchmark themselves or fork it, it’s on GitHub , so I encourage you to go nuts. I’ll happily report your results here (along with any mistakes or flaws you may find). My goal here is not to write the end-all-be-all benchmark for “I’m a vibe-coder, which framework should I choose?” The point of this post is to demonstrate that it’s possible in the era of AI coding to still make decisions based on evidence rather than vibes. The benchmark itself is largely vibe-coded, although I did review the code, so if there are mistakes then please consider them mine. I’d also be perfectly happy to see competitor frameworks try to improve on what I’ve done here. I’m also not trying to vilify any particular framework. I didn’t know which one would “win” before running the benchmark, although I did suspect that MPAs would outperform SPAs (which I’ve cheerfully admitted throughout this post). You could certainly write a more SPA-favored benchmark by making the app a complex dashboard, a video game, a productivity app, etc. You could also pick different metrics: Lighthouse and the Core Web Vitals are pretty tough on SPAs, so you could measure in-app interactivity instead. I’m also sure that the framework authors themselves could improve their frameworks or AI tools and do better on this benchmark. I have a strong suspicion, for example, that the current crop of MCPs and skills may be doing more harm than good. So if this post is the last word on these frameworks’ performance, I’ll be sorely disappointed. I’m sure there are also emerging frameworks that are champing at the bit to do well on benchmarks such as this one. If nothing else, I hope this post inspires you to apply additional scrutiny to your choice of JavaScript framework in this weird new era of vibe coding. Are you really picking your tech stack based on evidence? Or are you just going with what you already know? That’s certainly understandable, especially if you’re still reading, reviewing, and debugging the code yourself. But if you’ve gone largely hands-free, then what attachment do you really have to the choices you made back when you were typing code line-by-line like an animal? If you’re re-evaluating the entire way you build software, maybe it’s worth re-evaluating what you type after npm install ? Just saying. Personally, I don’t have any attachment to the frameworks I’ve evaluated above, except that I believe we should strive to build the best possible experiences for our users. I know and respect many of the authors of the above frameworks, and I know that they are working tirelessly for the same values I champion. My hope is just to push the entire community in a better direction toward better, faster, and more accessible frameworks to power the next generation of web apps. Addendum Framework versions used in the test (note Qwik had a patch release partway through the test): Framework Version Angular @angular/core 22.2.3 Astro astro 7.4.2 Gracile+Lit @gracile/gracile 0.11.0, lit 3.3.3 Hono+htmx hono 4.13.14, htmx.org 2.0.11 Next.js next 16.4.3, react 19.3.1 Nuxt nuxt 4.6.2, vue 3.5.44 Qwik @builder.io/qwik-city 1.20.2 (iteration 1), 1.20.3 (iterations 2, 3, 4, 5), @builder.io/qwik 1.20.2 (iteration 1), 1.20.3 (iterations 2, 3, 4, 5) React Router react-router 8.5.0, react 19.3.1 SolidStart @solidjs/start 2.1.0, solid-js 1.9.17 SvelteKit @sveltejs/kit 3.1.0, svelte 5.57.2 TanStack Start @tanstack/react-start 1.169.4, react 19.3.1 Vanilla vite 8.3.5 Update: an earlier version of this post overstated the Angular agents’ inability to build a working app. I’ve clarified the number of iterations per metric and reworded the post to avoid ambiguity. title: OccupySaaS
body_text: OccupySaaS — They laid us off. We're rebuilding their SaaS. Skip to content Occupy SaaS Why Method Projects Next FAQ Discord GitHub Est. October 2026 · Apache-2.0 They laid us off. We're rebuilding their SaaS. OccupySaaS is a protest movement written in code. Laid-off engineers, armed with AI and public documentation, are building clean-room, open-source, drop-in replacements for the platforms that rent our own industry back to us — one seat at a time. See the first releases Join the occupation We are the 1,000,000 Open source Clean room Drop-in compatible Self-hosted No per-seat tax Your data, your servers Fork the 1% Spec, not stolen code Open source Clean room Drop-in compatible Self-hosted No per-seat tax Your data, your servers Fork the 1% Spec, not stolen code The grievances The software built by the 99% belongs to the 99%. In 2011, Occupy Wall Street asked who the economy was really working for. In 2026 we're asking the same question about the cloud. The tools every company runs on are now toll booths — and the people who built them were shown the door. Per-seat pricing is a tax on growth Every hire, every intern, every contractor — another line item. Infrastructure shouldn't charge rent by the head. Lock-in is not a feature Proprietary APIs, export walls and surprise price hikes keep customers captive. Compatible open alternatives set them free. They cut us. We commit . A million engineers were let go while the platforms kept growing. We still know how to ship. Now we ship it in the open. The method Clean room. AI rebuild. Drop-in. We don't leak, decompile or copy anyone's code. Every project is rebuilt from public documentation and open standards, with AI doing the heavy lifting on the build side of a strict firewall — then proven compatible against the vendors' own public SDKs. Read the public record Public API references, open standards (OAuth 2.0, OIDC, REST) and published SDK behaviour become a written specification. Nothing confidential, nothing leaked, nothing from former employers. Raise the firewall Spec writers and builders stay separated. Each repo carries a CLEAN_ROOM.md policy, and provenance is recorded for every fixture and reference. Rebuild with AI AI agents implement from the spec alone — contracts first ( openapi.yaml ), then code, then tests — under human review at every merge. Prove compatibility A compatibility laboratory runs the vendors' own public client SDKs against our server. If your existing code doesn't work unchanged, it isn't done. Release it to everyone Apache-2.0. Self-hostable. Pluggable storage. No telemetry you didn't ask for, and no seat counter. Allowed in → Public API docs Open standards & RFCs Public SDK behaviour Black-box test results Clean room × Never allowed Leaked or proprietary source Decompiled binaries Former-employer confidential info Copied UI assets or trademarks First releases Two towers occupied. Identity and CRM: the two subscriptions almost every company pays for and almost nobody loves. Both are early, both are public, and both welcome contributors today. Early · in the open Go Zero Authy Replaces Auth0 A self-hostable identity server that speaks the Auth0 Authentication API. Point an existing Auth0 SDK at a ZeroAuthy tenant domain and it works with no code changes. OIDC discovery, JWKS & multi-tenant domains Hosted login, authorization code + PKCE client_credentials , rotating refresh tokens, revoke & logout Verified with auth0-spa-js, auth0-react & nextjs-auth0 # build & run $ go build -o bin/zeroauthy ./cmd/zeroauthy $ ./bin/zeroauthy serve --config config.yaml $ curl https://localhost:8443/.well-known/openid-configuration SQLite PostgreSQL MySQL gRPC plugins Apache-2.0 View on GitHub Clean-room policy Early · in the open Go · Vue · TypeScript Sales Compel Replaces Salesforce A free, open-source Salesforce replacement with a tenant-isolated Go/PostgreSQL core, a Vue record editor, and a compatibility laboratory that checks behaviour against Salesforce's public API contract. Persistent Account & Contact CRUD Object describe and limited queries External-ID upsert & bearer authentication OpenAPI 3.2 REST contract & offline test lab # run the compatibility laboratory $ npm ci --prefix compat/clients/node --ignore-scripts $ npm --prefix compat/clients/node run check PostgreSQL Multi-tenant REST i18n Apache-2.0 View on GitHub Clean-room policy The occupation map Who's next? Every category on this board is a monthly invoice somewhere. The movement picks the next target in public — bring a spec, a use case, or a grudge. ● Occupied Identity & Auth ZeroAuthy — Auth0-compatible login, tokens and tenants. ● Occupied CRM SalesCompel — Salesforce-compatible records and REST API. ○ Proposed Docs & Wikis Team knowledge bases that don't lock your writing behind a seat licence. ○ Proposed Issue Tracking Tickets, sprints and boards with a compatible API for existing integrations. ○ Proposed Feature Flags SDK-compatible flag evaluation you can run next to your own services. ○ Proposed Observability Logs, metrics and traces without per-gigabyte ransom notes. ○ Proposed Customer Support Help desk, inbox and knowledge base, priced at zero agents. + Your pick Propose a target Open an issue and make the case. Proposed categories are open for discussion, not commitments. Names of existing products are used only to describe compatibility. Lineage From Zuccotti Park to git push. Occupy Wall Street began on 17 September 2011 in Zuccotti Park, New York City, with a simple frame: the 1% and the 99%. It had no leaders, made decisions in open assemblies, and spread to hundreds of cities. OccupySaaS borrows that spirit and swaps tents for terminals. No marches, no property damage — just working software, published under an open licence, that anyone can run. “We are the 99%.” — Occupy Wall Street, 2011 17 Sep 2011 Occupy Wall Street begins Protesters set up camp in Zuccotti Park in Manhattan's Financial District. Oct 2011 The movement spreads Occupy camps and general assemblies appear in cities around the world. 15 Nov 2011 Zuccotti Park is cleared The camp ends; the language of the 1% and the 99% doesn't. 2022 – 2025 The great tech layoffs Wave after wave of cuts across the industry while subscription prices keep climbing. 14 Oct 2026 ZeroAuthy goes public The first clean-room rebuild opens its repo under Apache-2.0. 15 Oct 2026 SalesCompel joins the occupation The second tower. More to come — decided in the open. Join Occupy everything. You don't need permission, a badge or a manager. You need a laptop and an afternoon. Write code Pick an open issue, follow the clean-room policy, open a pull request. Self-host it Run a release against your real SDKs and tell us exactly where it breaks. Write specs Turn public docs into precise, testable specifications for the builders. Make noise Star the repos, share the site, and tell your CFO what you're paying per seat. Join on GitHub Join on Discord Donate via Buy Me a Coffee Propose a target Questions Fair questions. Is this legal? Clean-room reimplementation is a long-established way to build compatible software: you work only from public information and independently write your own code. Interoperating with an API is not the same as copying a product. Each project publishes its clean-room policy and source provenance so anyone can check the work. This page isn't legal advice; if you're adopting a project for a business, talk to your own counsel. Are you affiliated with Auth0, Okta or Salesforce? No. OccupySaaS and its projects are independent and not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by any vendor named on this site. Product names are used only to describe compatibility. Can former employees of those companies contribute? Yes, but never with confidential knowledge from a former employer. Contributors work only from public material, and anyone with relevant inside knowledge should stay on the public-spec side of the firewall or sit that project out. When in doubt, read the project's CLEAN_ROOM.md and ask first. Why use AI to build it? Because the giants had thousands of engineers and we have a movement. AI agents let a small group turn a precise spec into working code quickly. Humans write the specs, review every change, and own the result, and compatibility tests against real SDKs decide what counts as done. Why Go? Portability. A Go project compiles to a single self-contained binary, so self-hosting means dropping one file onto a server or into a Docker or Podman image — no installer, no runtime to set up, no tree of shared libraries to keep in sync. The same toolchain cross-compiles for Linux, macOS, Windows, x86 and ARM, and the result fits in a minimal container image. If you're leaving a SaaS vendor, the replacement should be this easy to carry. Why not Rust? Nothing is wrong with Rust, and we're not against it. Go was picked for the first projects because it makes the one-file, container-friendly drop-in the default with very little build setup. Rust can get there too; Go just gets there more simply for the kind of servers we're building. Rust recreations of these projects are welcome — they just haven't been made yet. The specs, API contracts and compatibility tests are language-neutral, so a Rust port can be checked against the same SDKs. If you want to start one, open an issue and say which project. Is it production-ready? Not yet. Both first projects are early and say so plainly in their READMEs, along with exactly which features work today. Try them, break them, and file issues. What does it cost? Nothing. Every project is released under the Apache License 2.0. Run it, fork it, sell services around it. The only thing we ask is that you contribute back what you can. Occupy SaaS A movement for the laid-off developers of the world: clean-room, open-source rebuilds of the software that runs everything.
