title: Digital minimalism
body_text: Dark Mode Toggle Digital minimalism 2026 Oct 31 See all posts Digital minimalism For a long time I have been a fan of minimalism in my physical life: have few physical possessions, and try to do more with less. Four years ago, I wrote this blog post describing what I had in the 40-liter backpack that I travel around with. Physical minimalism, however, was an idea that came of age in the 2000s and 2010s and was responding to the challenges and the opportunities of the 2000s and 2010s. I continue to believe that it is valuable - though I recognize some arguments in the other direction, notably that having the right kinds of physical things can make more practical to have more self-sovereignty over your life. But I also think that in the modern era, we need a new kind of minimalism: digital minimalism . Digital minimalism is about being intentional about ways that you access digital technology, making each use a conscious choice rather than something that you get sucked into by default. In this post, I will describe some experiments that I've done in this direction. Social media minimalism Twitter (aka X) has always had a strain of toxicity to it, that has been increasing in recent years. The platform is definitely engaging , but it's often far from informative , and the ways in which it engages often do not make you feel good . But this all seemed to hit a particular crescendo for me around the end of 2024 and beginning of 2025. Many things were happening at that moment, but if you spent a lot of time on X you will likely remember a particular one: everyone seemed to be suddenly becoming fans of Adolf Hitler . This is not even mentioning the time that Grok itself briefly turned into "MechaHitler" . Around the same time, "Crypto Twitter" was spiraling into a mood that I saw described as "financial nihilism": roughly, that the natural end state of blockchains is gambling, this is good, and if you dislike this and wish for something better then you are a stuck-up elitist prick. Naturally, I had (and continue to have) my intellectual disagreements with both of these trends. But on top of that, I also started to more seriously pay attention to the fact that while the style of discourse on the platform was engaging , it was not enlightening and not making me feel good . And so for much of this year, I have been doing an experiment in distancing myself somewhat from this chaos. I did not leave X the platform , but I did leave X the interface . Instead, I have been doing most of my tweeting through Firefly : Firefly is a multi-client that combines together X, BlueSky as well as Farcaster and Lens (both partially-Ethereum-based decentralized social media platforms). You can see tweets from all four platforms, and you can make a tweet that gets auto-posted to all four platforms. My primary goal in doing this was to support decentralized social media, and to continue to engage with X but in a way that distributes network effect rather than locking it in. But in my months of using Firefly, I found that it also has a different effect: I feel much better using it . I suspect the primary reason is that while Firefly allows you to tweet, and see other people's tweets, it is missing one central part of the X interface: The Algorithmâ¢ . In particular, I suspect that in my time using the X interface, I fell into the following trap: See someone making a tweet supportive of Adolf Hitler. Click on the tweet and look around its quotes and responses, the same way that someone would morbidly stare at a car accident. The Algorithmâ¢ thinks: "This user seems to be a fan of Adolf Hitler. Let me mark that down as one of his interests." See ten tweets supportive of Adolf Hitler. Click and look around with morbid curiosity, the same way that someone would morbidly stare if they saw for the first time a car accident where ten cars were crashed and burning at the same time. The Algorithmâ¢ thinks: ... well, you get the idea. See a hundred tweets supportive of Adolf Hitler. Now, in fairness to X and Elon and its hard-working employees, the Adolf Hitler fandom does seem to have greatly wound down in the one and a half years since then. I suspect part of this is because such movements inevitably burn out once people realize how immoral and stupid they are. But another part is undoubtedly genuine improvements in how The Algorithmâ¢ works. But even still , in those moments when I go back into the X interface, I find myself logging back out and going back to Firefly. I also find that my mind has changed. I find myself less interested in the various battles that the intellectual titans on the platform seem to be sucking every day of their lives into. Recently, I logged back in, and I learned that the culture war issue du jour was that people were stridently arguing about whether or not Mao was evil. When I saw this, I had an emotional response that was sort of similar to what I think is the common experience of being an adult, seeing some food or TV show or game that you used to love as a kid, and realizing that you now find no interest in it at all. I smiled, and immediately went back to enjoying my day. My verdict: I recommend more people try this. Explore ways of greatly decreasing or scoping your social media use: use something like Firefly, access X only on Tuesdays, whatever works for you. Get the information benefits of the platform without getting sucked in to the vortex, which does operate on you in powerful subconscious ways that you may not realize. Cell data minimalism For a period of 100 days, I embarked upon a second experiment: I lived my life with my phone always on airplane mode. I still used wifi, but not my cell connection. I had two goals in doing this: Privacy . A phone connected to cell is an always-on tracking device. Cell companies are notoriously bad at keeping that data secure, and sometimes they themselves sell it . So there is a large chance that a trail of your location will end up in the hands of intelligence agencies, military contractors, advertising companies, and more. Anonymous SIM cards are not a sufficient solution, for two reasons: (i) your phone can still be linked across its entire usage lifetime through its IMEI number, and (ii) you leak all kinds of data that can be used to reconstruct who you are from your fine-grained movement patterns, internet access patterns, and modern AI makes it very practical to uncover these patterns. Hence, the best location privacy solution is not having a cell connection at all (also, use GrapheneOS, and be very limited in what apps you give location permissions to; I had already been doing both). Mental health . Not having the internet at all for significant periods of time (when I'm outside) has been a good way of (re-)building the habit of surviving without it, and getting more mental peace and the space to think about other more healthy and productive things. On the whole, I consider the experiment to have been a success. During those 100 days, I violated the "no cell data" rule once literally but not spiritually - I turned it on briefly to receive a confirmation code that I needed in order to maintain that phone plan itself, and once spiritually but not literally - when going on a remote and slightly dangerous hike, friends insisted that I bring along a few communication devices that they had for emergency comms and use them to check in once every few hours. My largest inconvenience was a stretch of time I was in Singapore, when my inability to receive SMS confirmation codes meant that I could not log into Grab (the regional Uber equivalent). As a result, my food options were more limited, and I had to take the subway instead of a car even in situations where that was much more inconvenient. Since those 100 days, I have opened the cell connection occasionally, but so far I have broadly continued an "airplane mode by default" lifestyle. For navigation, I used CoMaps , a local-first mapping application that downloads OpenStreetMap data and then shows you a map, gives you directions to get where you need, etc locally. My general review of CoMaps is that I find it worse than Google Maps for navigating the human world (restaurants, stores, opening hours...) but better for navigating the natural-ish world (it knows about many trails that Google Maps does not, though it does occasionally fail by claiming trails that do not actually exist, leaving me on one occasion pushing through hundreds of meters of shrubbery to get back to civilization). I also became interested in the concept of local world knowledge apps. In principle, the data size of meaningful packs of information about the whole world is not that large. Compressed English wikipedia (without media) is only 27 GB . OpenStreetMap's planet.asm is 2.2 TB, though you can doubtlessly prune that down to 1-10% of its size and have everything you might conceivably need. This month there was a bounty (organized by Statuette; I contributed as one of the donors) to create local phone apps that try to make useful knowledge easily accessible offline. Here are two of the apps: Left: FieldAtlas . Right: Commonplace My general impression is: right now, we are exactly on the cusp of these kinds of apps starting to make sense. Most of the participants in the competition were trying to use on-device text LLMs to think for a long time before coming up with an answer. My impression is that this approach was too slow: answering a single question would take anywhere from 1 to 22 minutes. The best apps, on the other hand, used some kind of semantic search to show the user a search result from the local database immediately, and then followed that up with a very small LLM writing a text answer. This gives actually-good answers in a very reasonable timeframe. Finally, when you're out and about, especially if you have meetings, sometimes you do need to have internet when you're on the go. When you arrive at a place, you often need to contact a person you're meeting to confirm their exact location or to get them to open the door. When you're at one meeting, you often need to re-confirm details about the next. If you don't have cell data, your only option is public wifi - and importantly, the public wifi hotspot must allow you to connect without providing an SMS confirmation code. Different places are very different in terms of how friendly they are. Here is a quick tier list, taken from places I've traveled to while I was paying attention to public wifi availability: Taiwan (or at least, the Taipei area) Taipei has a huge number of public wifi hotspots. When I opened my phone to check when walking outside (or even when inside an Uber), there was literally an over 25% chance that there was a hotspot I could connect to that was in range at that moment. Usually, these were either municipal government wifi, or public wifi run by local convenience store chains. Ukraine, USA, Canada, Singapore Ukraine was the most surprising for me. In a surprisingly large number of places, across multiple cities, there were open hotspots available, some of which did not even require a clickthrough. (If you're wondering if it's responsible for them to do this, given Ukraine's security needs, I suspect the answer is that they are primarily concerned about decreasing the enemy's internet access near the frontline and on drones flying at high speed through the air toward their cities, and street-level wifi is not really useful for either of those) USA, Canada and Singapore were all similar: they had a very high number of theoretically-public wifi hotspots in general, but a large portion of those hotspots were gated behind either SMS or some kind of login. But even still, a very significant number of open wifi hotspots were available. Also, I learned that Toronto has a fraternity (or sorority) that seems to be named after SBF. Austria, Hungary Both halves of Charles I's old empire are similar. There are many hotspots, but the great majority of the public ones require an SMS confirmation code to log in. I could find properly open wifi, but on several occasions it took trying quite a few hotspots and walking around for a while. Switzerland Despite its general reputation for privacy, Switzerland ranked at the bottom for me. Almost all public wifi hotspots require an SMS confirmation code. In my first 1.5 kilometers walking through the downtown, I found only two that do not: a random shoe store, and Starbucks, which lets you connect for 10 minutes, and then longer if you enter a confirmation code that you receive by email. Web minimalism Recently, I have been starting to do more and more things without relying on user interfaces inside of websites at all. The last few times I updated my IPFS hash on ENS, I did so through a command-line tool that an AI wrote for me. Many of the payments that I make through privacy protocols, I now make through the kohaku-cli tool . Sending through kohaku-cli. Today, the CLI is even cleaner and easier to use; no need to specify the value twice and know what a tail call is. Websites and web applications, especially web applications for doing crypto things, are dangerous for several reasons: If you access a web application, you end up re-downloading the application from the server thousands of times, and you are fully trusting the server each time . If the server gets hacked even one of the thousands of times that you open the site, you might be screwed. Regular old-fashioned applications (where you explicitly click "download") are better than this: you only need to trust the server to not be malicious or hacked at that exact moment once. Websites and web applications are by default very bad for privacy . When you access a website, it can see your browser (including version number), your operating system, your screen size, and once you start acting hundreds of other data points (eg. mouse movements, button click patterns) that quickly identify you. Websites often send user data (and metadata) to all kinds of third-party providers, from CDNs serving scripts to analytics companies, and this all happens by default. As we've seen with social media, web applications crafted by third parties with commercial interests may not have your interests at heart. Fine-grained UI decisions may be dark patterns optimized to extract, whereas what you want is bright patterns that are optimized to enlighten and educate and protect you. So what's the alternative? Basically, bring back the Unix Philosophy , but make it better and much more user-friendly with local AI: speak English to tell your computer what to do rather than Bash. At its core, the Unix philosophy was simple: make simple, modular tools that each do one thing and one thing well, and that are designed to talk to each other through the most universal interface (text). You as a user have extremely fine-grained choice about how to make the different programs fit together. UIs, on the other hand, combine many functionalities into one single opaque tool produced by a single developer. At their apex, UIs turned into "super-apps", which greatly concentrate power in the application developer and have complex and unintelligible internal workings, magnifying security risks. With LLMs, we can go back to the Unix philosophy approach, putting the fine-grained decision-making power back into the user's hands, but without the downside of everyone needing to become a programmer. Conclusion Physical-world minimalism, of the style that became popular in the 2000s and 10s, was made possible by a new wave of technology: computers and the internet. A single computer could substitute for dozens of physical things. As a result, you could live a life of much greater simplicity and freedom, with just a laptop, a few sets of clothing, and basic charging and hygiene equipment. Physical minimalism was much harder before the internet; it was doable, but would entail a much more complex lifestyle commitment. After the internet, the costs of a more physically minimalistic lifestyle greatly dropped. With the last ten years of progress of software quality, together with modern AI, I would argue that we now have the wave of technology needed to similarly enable the next wave of minimalism: digital minimalism. We need social media less than before, because you can talk to the bot for information instead (and for human connection, there's still the old-fashioned solution: going out and talking to people in real life). We need the internet less than before, because there's so much more you can do purely locally and offline. And we need the web less than before, because you can do much more, and more conveniently, though either command-line tools or custom-made user interfaces, and AI can help you use or craft both. And these things are all happening at exactly the time that the flaws of these previous paradigms - and, for that matter, the flaws of using AI in the wrong way - are reaching their apex, and so a digital minimalism is becoming more and more necessary. Each person's path to digital minimalism will be different, as each person has different needs. But I highly recommend everyone try reducing their digital clutter in at least one important way, and if you like the result then keep going.

It displays the real-time positions of stars, planets, constellations, and more, all within your terminal—no telescope required! Configure sky views by date, time, and location with precise ASCII-rendered visuals. See usage for all supported options! astroterm is constantly improving, and we'd love to hear your ideas! If you have a suggestion or find a bug, please open an issue and share your feedback. See CONTRIBUTING.md for guidelines on building, testing, and contributing to astroterm . The night sky above Singapore on January 2, 2025 See usage on how to obtain this view Table of Contents 🌌 astroterm Features Installation Usage Troubleshooting Citations Data Sources Features 🔭 Highly Customizable: Choose any date, time, and location to explore past, present, or future celestial events 📐 Accurate Rendering: View the moon, stars, and planets with as much precision as terminal graphics allow 🌘 Moon Phases: Precise lunar phases in real-time 🌌 Constellation Figures: Detailed constellation shapes ⚡ Performance Optimized: Lightweight and fast ASCII rendering Stars over Sydney, Australia on January 6, 2025 Installation Several installation methods are provided based on your platform. If none of these fit your needs, you can always build from source . Refer to troubleshooting for help resolving any issues. Arch Linux You can install astroterm from the extra repository using pacman : pacman -S astroterm Fedora You can install astroterm directly from the Fedora package repository on Fedora 40+. sudo dnf install astroterm Homebrew You can install astroterm from Homebrew via: brew install astroterm Nix You can try the package in a temporary environment with the following command: nix-shell -I nixpkgs=channel:nixpkgs-unstable -p astroterm --command astroterm Argument flags are added by wrapping the command in quotes. For example: nix-shell -I nixpkgs=channel:nixpkgs-unstable -p astroterm --command " astroterm -u -c " To make astroterm available from your $PATH , add it to your configuration.nix: environment.systemPackages = with pkgs ; [ ... astroterm ] Guix You can install astroterm directly from the Guix main channel starting from this commit . guix time-machine --commit=4b5f0408e66392ab745dc0f7830732217d88f17d -- shell astroterm Or after guix pull : guix shell astroterm -- astroterm --help # to try guix package --install astroterm # add to current profile Prebuilt Executable Unix Download the latest executable using wget wget -O astroterm " https://github.com/da-luce/astroterm/releases/latest/download/astroterm-<os>-<arch> " Replace <os> with the appropriate platform: Linux: linux macOS: darwin Replace <arch> with the appropriate architecture: Linux: x86_64 (arm64 support to come after Ubuntu arm64 runners are available) Apple Silicon (M-series): aarch64 Intel-based Macs: x86_64 To view all supported combinations, see the Releases page. Run the executable chmod +x ./astroterm ./astroterm Windows Download the latest .exe file using PowerShell's Invoke-WebRequest : Invoke-WebRequest - Uri " https://github.com/da-luce/astroterm/releases/latest/download/astroterm-win-x86_64.exe " - OutFile " astroterm.exe " Run the .exe .\ astroterm.exe Building From Source Usage Options The --help flag displays all supported options: Usage: astroterm [OPTION]... -a, --latitude=<degrees> Observer latitude [-90°, 90°] (default: 0.0) -o, --longitude=<degrees> Observer longitude [-180°, 180°] (default: 0.0) -d, --datetime=<yyyy-mm-ddThh:mm:ss> Observation datetime in UTC -t, --threshold=<float> Only render stars brighter than this magnitude (default: 5.0) -l, --label-thresh=<float> Label stars brighter than this magnitude (default: 0.25) -f, --fps=<int> Frames per second (default: 24) -s, --speed=<float> Animation speed multiplier (default: 1.0) -c, --color Enable terminal colors -C, --constellations Draw constellation stick figures. Note: a constellation is only drawn if all stars in the figure are over the threshold -g, --grid Draw an azimuthal grid -u, --unicode Use unicode characters -b, --braille Use braille characters for constellation lines (requires Unicode) -q, --quit-on-any Quit on any keypress (default is to quit on 'q' or 'ESC' only) -m, --metadata Display metadata -r, --aspect-ratio=<float> Override the calculated terminal cell aspect ratio. Use this if your projection is not 'square.' A value around 2.0 works well for most cases -h, --help Print this help message -B, --bash-completions Print bash completions -i, --city=<city_name> Use the latitude and longitude of the provided city. If the name contains multiple words, enclose the name in single or double quotes. For a list of available cities, see: https://github.com/da-luce/astroterm/blob/main/data/ cities.csv -v, --version Display version info and exit Shell Completions To enable Tab completions in Bash, add the following line to your ~/.bashrc : source <( astroterm --bash-completions ) Example 1 To achieve the "spinning globe" effect as shown in the README GIF , use the following flags: astroterm --color --constellations --speed 10000 --fps 64 --city Singapore or astroterm -cC -s 10000 -f 64 -i Singapore for short. In fact, any city around the equator will work. Locations closer to the poles will look different because the apparent motion of the stars is more circular around the celestial pole rather than sweeping across the sky. Example 2 Say we wanted to view the sky at 5:00 AM (Eastern) on July 16, 1969—the morning of the Apollo 11 launch at the Kennedy Space Center in Florida. We would run: astroterm --latitude 28.573469 --longitude -80.651070 --datetime 1969-7-16T8:00:00 Finding the precise coordinates can be cumbersome, so we could also use the nearest major city to achieve a similar result: astroterm --city Orlando --datetime 1969-7-16T8:00:00 -m While we're still waiting for someone to invent time travel, we can cheat a little by using Stellarium to confirm that this aligns with reality. If we then wanted to display constellations and add color, we would add --constellations --color as options. If you simply want the current time, don't specify the --datetime option and astroterm will use the system time. For your current location, you will still have to specify the --lat and --long options, or provide the nearest city with the --city option. For more options and help, run astroterm -h or astroterm --help . Tip Use a tool like LatLong to get your latitude and longitude. Tip Star magnitudes decrease as apparent brightness increases, i.e., to show more stars, increase the threshold. Troubleshooting Release Won't Download via Curl For some reason, curl does not follow the latest release redirect. Use wget to download the latest release or hardcode the tag in the link using curl . Or, just download via the releases page . Broken Unicode on Linux If Unicode characters do not display correctly in the terminal, you may need to configure your system's locale to support Unicode. Temporarily set the locale (add this to ~/.bashrc or equivalent to permanently enforce) export LC_ALL= " en_US.UTF-8 " export LC_CTYPE= " en_US.UTF-8 " Install and configure locales (example for Ubuntu/Debian) sudo apt update sudo apt install -y locales sudo dpkg-reconfigure locales During configuration, select en_US.UTF-8 as the default locale. title: Northflank Breached
body_text: Northflank - Status Northflank - Status Page Get updates Email Slack Microsoft Teams Discord Google Chat Webhook RSS Atom API Get updates Email Slack Microsoft Teams Discord Google Chat Webhook RSS Atom API Preferences Appearance Experiencing partial outage Security incident Monitoring · Major outage Monitoring · November 02, 2026 at 11:09 AM UTC We believe the attack vector was contained within an hour of the first alert. Our investigation shows no sign that the attacker was in our environment after the attack. Independent forensic auditors began reviewing the attack together with Northflank over the weekend, and they continue to review it. Impact on your workloads Running workloads were unaffected. At this time we have seen no sign that workloads or workload data were accessed during the attack. Evidence suggests it was focused on secrets held in our control plane. Customers on forward-deployed or dedicated control planes are unaffected. Separately, we have patched CVE-2026-98432 across our fleet, including BYOC clusters where we have an active integration. If your BYOC cluster is no longer connected to Northflank, please contact support. Over the last few days there has been intermittent platform degradation while we rotated our own keys and hardened the platform. What you need to do Some customers have reported unauthorised use of AI secrets. Please rotate all secrets now, both integration secrets and project secrets, even if you haven’t seen suspicious activity. We recommend starting with AI provider keys, cloud provider credentials, payment provider keys, private keys, and database and other service credentials. We also recommend reviewing your provider logs for unusual activity. If you have seen unexpected AI usage or spend, contact your AI providers directly, such as OpenAI and Anthropic. Where we were able to act on your behalf, we have revoked Northflank access tokens and sessions, VCS integrations, and cross-account IAM roles and service accounts. If you haven’t already, sign in again and reconnect your integrations. Need help? If you need help rotating secrets or checking that everything has been rotated, contact support@northflank.com , or use your direct channel with us if you have one. We are treating this with the utmost urgency, and the entire organisation has been working 24/7. What’s next We will keep updating this page as the review progresses, and we intend to share a root cause analysis once we have confirmed findings. Update · October 31, 2026 at 11:31 PM UTC Secret rotation is now available for RabbitMQ add-ons for all customers. Please rotate all secrets if you have not already. Update · October 31, 2026 at 10:32 PM UTC Secret rotation for Minio Addons is now available to all customers. Please rotate all secrets if you have not already. Update · October 31, 2026 at 1:34 PM UTC Secret rotation for MySQL and Redis is now available to all customers. Please rotate all secrets if you have not already. Update · October 31, 2026 at 1:04 AM UTC We have enabled audit logs for all customers, including free users. Update · October 30, 2026 at 11:38 PM UTC Users have reported unauthorised use of AI API keys supplied to the Northflank platform. If you have not already rotated your user-provided secrets stored in Northflank, please do so immediately. Revoke existing credentials with their issuing providers, generate replacements, and update the affected secrets and workloads in Northflank. Review your AI provider usage and billing logs for unexpected activity, and report any suspicious usage to Northflank support and the relevant provider. These reports may be consistent with the broader pattern of attacks targeting AI credentials. Similar IP addresses are contained in this article  Wiz’s “Black October” report . Update · October 30, 2026 at 7:28 PM UTC Our investigation is ongoing. We have no further confirmed findings to share at this time. Our guidance remains unchanged: assume all environment variables have been compromised and rotate all secrets and credentials immediately, including those in workloads, secret groups and global secrets. Disable public access to addons where enabled. We will share further updates as more information is confirmed. Update · October 30, 2026 at 3:12 PM UTC Secret rotation on Postgres and MongoDB has been enabled for all users. We recommend disabling public expose on addons if you have enabled that. All users should assume their environment variables are decrypted and begin rotation immediately. Secrets on workloads Secret groups Global secrets Multiple users are confirming that their AI keys have been used. title: Leak Exposes 41,000 Homeland Security Workers–Including Undercover ICE Agents
body_text: Massive Leak Exposes 41,000 Homeland Security Workers—Including Undercover ICE Agents | WIRED Skip to main content THE WIRED APP IS HERE DOWNLOAD NOW » Menu WIRED SECURITY POLITICS THE BIG STORY BUSINESS SCIENCE CULTURE REVIEWS Menu WIRED Account Account Newsletters Security Politics The Big Story Business Science Culture Reviews Chevron More Expand The Big Interview Magazine Events WIRED Insider WIRED Consulting Newsletters Podcasts Video Livestreams WIRED Store Search Search Dhruv Mehrotra Maddy Varner Dell Cameron Security Oct 28, 2026 4:00 PM Massive Leak Exposes 41,000 Homeland Security Workers—Including Undercover ICE Agents The leaked records include the locations of ICE and CBP facilities, workers’ cell phone numbers, and the members of groups tied to wiretap programs, Palantir software, and xAI’s Grok chatbot. Photo-Illustration: Jobanny Cabrera; Getty Images Comment Loader Save Story Save this story Comment Loader Save Story Save this story An unprecedented leak of Department of Homeland Security records has exposed details of more than 41,000 employees or contractors who work for the department and its constituent agencies. The records include email addresses, phone numbers, and office addresses, but also references to internal systems and sensitive information on undercover and surveillance programs. In all, the leak provides a map of how DHS is organized and how it operates. The records, which span DHS itself as well as seven component agencies, including Immigration and Customs Enforcement and US Customs and Border Protection, were last updated on August 19, 2026. The transparency nonprofit Distributed Denial of Secrets and cybersecurity researcher and journalist maia arson crimew previewed the data for WIRED, which they say they obtained from a group calling itself the Department of Peace. DDoSecrets published the archive, which it calls “Icepick,” on Wednesday. In a press release, DDoSecrets says the data is from DHS's Okta login system. In a note with the files, the hackers wrote, “They have our information, so it’s only fair that we have theirs.” An Okta spokesperson tells WIRED that it is unaware of any breach of its systems. “We are aware of this report. Okta is secure, and we have no evidence our data or systems were compromised,” the spokesperson says. The leak comes as DHS has aggressively pursued its critics , seeking to unmask anonymous social media users, obtain customer records on protesters, and secure warrants for surveillance tools aimed at reporters. Since the start of the second Trump administration, DHS and the federal government have moved to hide DHS employees’ names and faces . The agency has also expanded its definition of “doxing”—a term that typically refers to publishing someone’s home address and other personal details for malicious purposes—to encompass the publication of basic facts about public employees, like their names and titles. The leak follows a breach in which a group of hackers known as ShinyHunters claimed to have stolen personal information on nearly every FBI employee and their families. Law enforcement agencies have arrested several suspects and detained another who is alleged to be part of the group. The DHS records are searchable on a website crimew built. “I don't think we should let them scare us into not looking into them,” she tells WIRED. “DHS is aware of a potential breach and is actively working to address the situation swiftly and effectively,” a Homeland Security spokesperson tells WIRED. “We take all security threats against our employees and officers seriously and will work to ensure all are properly protected. We will update the public when more information is available.” The DOJ did not respond to WIRED’s request for comment. The FBI referred WIRED’s inquiry to DHS. According to a WIRED analysis of the data, CBP staffers account for more than half of the records. ICE accounts for about 10,000, roughly a third of them in Homeland Security Investigations, ICE’s investigative wing. Another 6,200 belong to US Citizenship and Immigration Services, and nearly 1,000 are tied to the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, more than half of them contractors. Altogether, the files cover about a seventh of DHS’s workforce, revealing how DHS is structured, from senior leadership down to individual immigration agents and detention contractors. Like most large organizations, DHS uses permission groups to control access to internal systems, according to the leaked records. Nearly everyone named in the leak has access to at least some of these systems. At HSI, 39 employees across more than a dozen field offices belong to groups whose names include “CUC,” which government court filings say stands for “certified undercover operation.” Another group, apparently based in HSI's St. Paul, Minnesota, area of operations, references "Keyhole," which federal court filings describe as a certified undercover operation that recently funded HSI’s undercover surveillance of Minneapolis protest groups earlier this year. Others reference a “Communications Intercept Center TechOps (CICTO) Program,” a “Title III Intercept Program” for wiretaps, and an “Illicit Sensor Intercept Program (ISIP).” The names of the groups—there are over 55,000 in all—appear to reference tools for accessing immigration court records, pulling data from seized phones, and conducting surveillance. These include Palantir’s Falcon investigative platform and PenLink, which analyzes phone records and social media. Two permission groups, named “Executive Leadership” and “AI Access,” appear to list people given exceptions to DHS's web filter, which blocks some websites for employees. They contain the same 13 people, including former DHS head Kristi Noem; Antoine McCord, the recently departed DHS chief information officer who has returned to defense tech company Anduril ; Philip Hegseth, listed as a senior adviser to the DHS secretary and the younger brother of defense secretary Pete Hegseth; and Jayce Krachenfels, listed as a policy adviser, who previously worked as a regional field director for Donald Trump’s 2024 presidential campaign, according to his LinkedIn profile. Noem, McCord, Hegseth, and Krachenfels did not respond to a request for comment Other groups named in the leak reference AI tools, including OpenAI’s ChatGPT, Google’s Gemini, and Microsoft’s Copilot. One, called “Grok.com,” includes eight DHS technology officials, including the department’s former chief information officer and chief data officer. “If authentic and current, this is an extraordinarily valuable intelligence resource for those seeking to penetrate DHS,” says Alexander Leslie, a national security expert at the threat intelligence company Recorded Future. “This dataset becomes way more valuable when correlated with previously compromised information, commercial data, and other intelligence collections. An adversary could spend months exploiting these relationships to identify vulnerable personnel, develop convincing impersonation attempts, or compromise ongoing investigations.” More than 700 accounts are associated with a group apparently referencing Signal , the encrypted messaging app, nearly all belonging to CBP personnel. More than 200 CBP accounts belong to a group referencing Mobile Fortify , a face-recognition app that immigration agents use to identify people. The group includes field supervisors, special response team operators, and tactical and intelligence agents. About half are in Texas, California, and Arizona. Roughly 1,300 ICE enforcement accounts have been created since July 4, 2025, when Trump signed the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which funded the hiring of 10,000 new ICE Enforcement and Removal officers by the end of 2025. Nearly 20 accounts appear to belong to personnel with the Department of Defense, which the administration styles as the Department of War; eight are in a group titled “ICE Tip Line DOW Surge.” About 170 accounts are listed as providing “military processing support” at ICE facilities, and 35 others explicitly identify National Guard members. Dozens of accounts have job titles like “Designated Immigration Officer” and “287(g) Officer,” which mark local law enforcement personnel authorized to carry out some immigration enforcement duties . Many list county sheriff's offices and jails as their workplaces. The records also include roughly 4,400 “associates,” whose jobs range from IT developers and data scientists to nurses and detention officers. Of those, 145 are named as a “contractor” or “high risk contractor.” More than 300 records reference senior titles associated with DHS headquarters, from Noem down through deputy undersecretaries, assistant secretaries, and chiefs of staff to officials overseeing intelligence, technology, biometrics, and privacy. Most records also name a supervisor, which could allow anyone analyzing the dataset to reconstruct reporting relationships across the department. The Trump administration has prosecuted protesters for posting information about individual ICE officers and warned others for doing so. In June, 15 Minnesota residents were charged under laws related to stalking and threats of violence, which prosecutors linked to their participation in ICE-opposition activities. More than 100 HSI agents , including undercover operatives, took part in an operation that included widespread surveillance and infiltration of group chats. Adam Steinbaugh, a senior attorney at the nonprofit civil liberties group FIRE, says that the Trump administration has taken an expansive view of 18 USC 119 , a law that prohibits people from sharing “restricted personal information” about federal officers or their families with the intent to threaten them. “This is information that would be on a business card,” says Steinbaugh of the names and basic work details included in the archive. “That’s not something the government can criminalize." Despite the potential sensitivity of other records in the leaked data, the creators of Icepick do not consider it doxing. They see it as an accountability tool. “The DHS especially as an agency completely lacks accountability, despite many parts of it being incredibly unpopular. The people who work there know this too; for example, some of their LinkedIn bios simply say ‘stuff at US Government,’” says crimew. “If they weren't hiding their involvement in the repressive arm of the US government, there would be no need for us to expose them in the first place.” Updated 10/28/2026 at 8:02 pm ET: Added comment from DHS.
